discovery.question: In your class photo, three friends who all turned 12 this year look wildly different — one looks 15, one looks 12, one still looks 10. A visiting aunt whispers, 'Someone must be lying about their age!' What's really going on?
options: Nothing is wrong — bodies grow in 'spurts' on their own schedules during adolescence
The tall one is secretly older — everyone grows the same amount each year
The shorter ones are sick — equal ages should mean equal heights
They look different only because they eat different brands of food
discovery.answer: Nothing is wrong — bodies grow in 'spurts' on their own schedules during adolescence
discovery.hook: Same age does not mean same stage. Adolescence has no school-wide timetable — each body starts and finishes on a schedule as unique as a fingerprint.

c6_biology_ch06.mission: Follow one student's body through a growth spurt — track the changes inside and out — and figure out why their best friend is still waiting for theirs.
c6_biology_ch06.finale: Adolescence isn't a race with a single start line. Your body is quietly rebuilding you for adulthood — on a schedule that's entirely your own.
c6_biology_ch06.subtitle: Why do classmates your age look so different from each other?
c6_biology_ch06.role: a growth detective puzzling over a class photo
c6_biology_ch06.intro: Three friends, all 12, look like they belong in three different grades. Somewhere between birthday candles and shoe sizes, adolescence is running on personal clocks.
c6_biology_ch06.goal: Explain why growth spurts hit different people at different times — and stop worrying that your body is 'late'.

discovery.question: Rohan is sure digestion happens in the stomach — 'that's why it growls!' His grandmother insists digestion starts the moment food enters the mouth. Who should win this argument?
options: Grandmother — chewing and saliva begin digestion in the mouth; the stomach is just one stop
Rohan — the stomach does all the digesting; the mouth only cuts food smaller
Both are wrong — digestion happens only in the intestines
Neither — food turns straight into energy inside the blood
discovery.answer: Grandmother — chewing and saliva begin digestion in the mouth; the stomach is just one stop
discovery.hook: Digestion is an assembly line, not a single machine. Mouth, stomach, intestine, liver and pancreas each add something before food can become energy.

c6_biology_ch09.mission: Escort a bite of roti from the first chew through the whole food-factory — past the acid bath of the stomach and the 'chemists' liver and pancreas — until it's absorbed.
c6_biology_ch09.finale: Your body never asks one organ to do a whole job. Digestion is a relay — and the race starts in your mouth, not your stomach.
c6_biology_ch09.subtitle: Trace a bite of food through the body's longest assembly line
c6_biology_ch09.role: a tiny food inspector riding through the digestive system
c6_biology_ch09.intro: A bite of aloo paratha is about to take the longest journey of its life — through a muscular tube where organs take turns breaking it down.
c6_biology_ch09.goal: Map every station of the digestive system and see why removing even one helper organ changes everything.

discovery.question: A dry chickpea sits unchanged in a cupboard for months. The same chickpea wrapped in a wet cloth sprouts in three days. The cupboard had air and warmth too — so what did the wet cloth unlock?
options: Water woke the seed — it swells, cracks its coat, and spends its stored food to grow
The cloth gave the seed special food the cupboard lacked
The cupboard was too dark — seeds need light before they can sprout
The wet cloth was warmer, and heat alone made it sprout
discovery.answer: Water woke the seed — it swells, cracks its coat, and spends its stored food to grow
discovery.hook: Seeds don't 'eat' the soil. A sprouting seed runs on a packed lunch — food stored in its cotyledons — until its own leaves open for business.

c6_biology_ch10.mission: Wake a sleeping seed yourself — give it exactly what it needs, then watch the root dive down and the shoot climb up toward light.
c6_biology_ch10.finale: A seed is a packed suitcase: food inside, instructions inside, waiting only for water to say 'go'. Soil comes later — the first meal is homemade.
c6_biology_ch10.subtitle: What does a sleeping seed need before it dares to grow?
c6_biology_ch10.role: a gardener with two bean seeds and one wet paper towel
c6_biology_ch10.intro: Two identical seeds, two bowls — one dry, one damp. In three days only one has sprouted. What secret did the water whisper?
c6_biology_ch10.goal: Discover what germination really needs, and bust the myth that baby plants eat soil.

discovery.question: Your school bag is cloth, your bottle is plastic, your window is glass — yet nobody makes windows from cloth or bags from glass. What test is everyone secretly running?
options: They match the material's properties — hardness, flexibility, transparency — to the job it must do
They simply use whichever material is cheapest that day
It's pure tradition — bags have always been cloth
They pick whichever material is most colourful
discovery.answer: They match the material's properties — hardness, flexibility, transparency — to the job it must do
discovery.hook: Every material has a 'personality' — shine, hardness, see-through-ness. Choosing materials is really matchmaking between properties and purpose.

c6_chemistry_ch04.mission: Sort a messy storeroom of mystery objects — test each for shine, hardness, solubility and transparency — then decide what each is fit to become.
c6_chemistry_ch04.finale: Glass for windows, cloth for bags — nothing is random. Once you can read a material's properties, every object in the room starts making sense.
c6_chemistry_ch04.subtitle: Why is your bottle plastic and your window glass?
c6_chemistry_ch04.role: a materials detective sorting a jumbled storeroom
c6_chemistry_ch04.intro: A pile of objects — keys, chalk, cloth, glass, salt — all mixed up. Each one is hiding clues in its shine, hardness and see-through-ness.
c6_chemistry_ch04.goal: Group materials by their properties and explain why coloured glass is still transparent.

discovery.question: You crumple a sheet of paper — still paper. You burn it — it becomes ash and smoke, and no amount of unfolding brings it back. What did the fire do that your hands couldn't?
options: It created entirely new substances — a chemical change; crumpling only changed the shape
It made a bigger mess — drastic changes are always chemical
Fire is hot, and hot changes are chemical while cold changes are physical
Nothing — ash is just paper in a different shape
discovery.answer: It created entirely new substances — a chemical change; crumpling only changed the shape
discovery.hook: Physical changes can be drastic and permanent — a glass shattered forever is still glass. The real question isn't 'can it change back?' but 'did something NEW appear?'

c6_chemistry_ch05.mission: Run a change-detective lab: sort melting ice, torn paper, rusting nails and burnt toast into 'same stuff' vs 'new stuff' — and defend every call.
c6_chemistry_ch05.finale: The shape can shatter, melt or shrink — but if no new substance appears, it's the same old stuff in disguise. New material means a chemical story.
c6_chemistry_ch05.subtitle: Same stuff in disguise, or brand-new substance?
c6_chemistry_ch05.role: a change detective in a kitchen full of mysteries
c6_chemistry_ch05.intro: Ice melting, chalk crushed to powder, a nail going orange with rust — your job is to decide which changes only dressed matter up and which truly transformed it.
c6_chemistry_ch05.goal: Separate physical from chemical changes using the one question that matters: did a new substance appear?

discovery.question: A new school rule says only children wearing a red badge may speak in class. No law forbids it — the principal simply decided. Can a rule be 'official' and still be wrong?
options: Yes — the right to speak and be treated equally belongs to everyone simply for being human
No — whatever the principal decides is automatically fair
Yes, but only because red is an unlucky colour
No — rights exist only when a rulebook grants them
discovery.answer: Yes — the right to speak and be treated equally belongs to everyone simply for being human
discovery.hook: Rights aren't prizes a government hands out — they're the rules of being human. A law that breaks them isn't strong law; it's a bully with paperwork.

c6_civics_ch10.mission: Put a suspicious new rulebook on trial — test each rule against human rights and strike down the ones that fail the fairness test.
c6_civics_ch10.finale: Rights don't come from governments — governments are judged by them. That's why even an official rule can still be wrong.
c6_civics_ch10.subtitle: Who gave you your rights — and who is allowed to take them?
c6_civics_ch10.role: a junior judge reviewing a school's unfair rulebook
c6_civics_ch10.intro: A new rulebook has landed: some children may speak, others may not. Your job is to test each rule — not against the law, but against what every human deserves.
c6_civics_ch10.goal: Tell the difference between a privilege someone grants and a right you were born with.

discovery.question: Ask a class 'Who is the government?' and most shout 'the Prime Minister!' But the PM can't personally fix your school tap, run the hospital and patrol the roads. So who — or what — is the government really?
options: A whole system — schools, hospitals, police, road departments — that makes rules and keeps services running
The PM and President alone — everyone else just works for them
Only the police, because they're the ones who enforce rules
The richest citizens, because they pay for the services
discovery.answer: A whole system — schools, hospitals, police, road departments — that makes rules and keeps services running
discovery.hook: The government is less like a single captain and more like the referee plus the entire stadium crew — a system, not a face on TV.

c6_civics_ch11.mission: Spend one day as the invisible manager of your town — keep water, roads, schools and safety running — and count how many 'governments' are really at work.
c6_civics_ch11.finale: One person never ran a country. The government is the whole crew behind the scenes — and you met it today in every tap, road and classroom.
c6_civics_ch11.subtitle: If the PM can't fix your school tap, who is the government?
c6_civics_ch11.intro: The taps run, the buses move, the school gate opens — someone is running all of it. Today that someone is you, and the government turns out to be everywhere.
c6_civics_ch11.goal: See government as a system of services, not a single leader.

discovery.question: A village has 200 children and zero swings. Should they write to the state capital and wait, or gather in the Gram Sabha and decide it themselves? Which path gets kids swinging sooner?
options: The Gram Sabha — the people closest to a problem can see it, discuss it and fix it fastest
The state government — bigger government always means better solutions
Neither — villages can't build anything without outside engineers
Write to the Prime Minister — the very top always decides best
discovery.answer: The Gram Sabha — the people closest to a problem can see it, discuss it and fix it fastest
discovery.hook: Democracy doesn't only live in faraway parliaments. Its roots are in your street — where neighbours meet, argue, decide and fix things together.

c6_civics_ch12.mission: Bring a broken-fence problem to the Gram Sabha — gather the villagers, hear every side, and steer the meeting toward a fix the whole village owns.
c6_civics_ch12.finale: Grassroots democracy isn't voting once in five years — it's neighbours solving problems all year round. Power planted close to the ground grows fastest.
c6_civics_ch12.subtitle: Why does the smallest government often solve the biggest local problems?
c6_civics_ch12.role: a Gram Sabha member with a broken fence to fix
c6_civics_ch12.intro: The playground fence is broken and the state office is 300 km away. Luckily, democracy has roots — and they reach right into your village square.
c6_civics_ch12.goal: Experience participation as everyday problem-solving, not just election-day voting.

discovery.question: The government announces it 'has a budget,' so a student concludes it must be saving money and shouldn't build the new road. What's wrong with this picture?
options: A budget isn't about not-spending — it's a plan for spending public money well
Nothing — having a budget means the government must stop all spending
The road is cancelled because roads are never allowed in budgets
Budgets are secret — nobody should even know about the road
discovery.answer: A budget isn't about not-spending — it's a plan for spending public money well
discovery.hook: A budget is a roadmap of money, not a lock on the wallet. It decides where every rupee goes — roads, schools, hospitals — before the year even starts.

c6_civics_ch13.mission: Balance one year of a country's money — collect the taxes, then split every rupee among hospitals, schools and roads — and defend your choices to the people.
c6_civics_ch13.finale: You don't budget to avoid spending — you budget so the spending makes sense. Every line in the plan is a promise about what the nation values most.
c6_civics_ch13.subtitle: A country's pocket-money plan, scaled up a billion times
c6_civics_ch13.role: a junior finance minister planning the year
c6_civics_ch13.intro: Taxes are in and requests are flooding — hospitals want machines, schools want roofs, farmers want roads. You hold the plan that decides it all.
c6_civics_ch13.goal: Read a budget as a plan for spending, not a rule against it.

discovery.question: A student sighs, 'Indians speak different languages, eat different food, pray differently — how can a country this different ever hold together?' What's the flaw in the worry?
options: Difference isn't division — people can live differently and still share one country and its rules
No flaw — countries must make everyone identical to survive
India holds together only because everyone secretly eats the same food
Different people get along only when they never meet each other
discovery.answer: Difference isn't division — people can live differently and still share one country and its rules
discovery.hook: Diversity means many ways of living under one roof — like different lunchboxes at one table. Difference is the menu, not the fight.

c6_civics_ch14.mission: Curate a school Diversity Fair — group languages, foods, festivals and dress into exhibits that show many lives adding up to one nation.
c6_civics_ch14.finale: Different languages, different lunches — same classroom, same rules, same country. Diversity isn't a crack in India's wall; it's the design.
c6_civics_ch14.subtitle: Many lunchboxes, one table — how difference holds a country together
c6_civics_ch14.role: curator of a school Diversity Fair
c6_civics_ch14.intro: Your classmates speak five languages at home and bring five different lunches — yet share one classroom and one flag. Your job: turn that variety into a fair.
c6_civics_ch14.goal: See diversity as richness to celebrate, not a problem to solve.

discovery.question: A country bans all newspapers, TV news and internet reports overnight — movies and music stay, but news is gone. Entertainment survives, so what is actually lost?
options: Citizens lose the facts they need to check the government — media is democracy's watchdog, not just fun
Nothing important — media was only ever entertainment anyway
Only celebrities lose the spotlight; ordinary citizens are unaffected
People lose TV, but the government automatically becomes more honest
discovery.answer: Citizens lose the facts they need to check the government — media is democracy's watchdog, not just fun
discovery.hook: Media is the messenger between rulers and ruled. Take it away and citizens can't see what the government is doing — and a government nobody watches can do anything.

c6_civics_ch15.mission: Run a newsroom for one hectic day — pick which stories citizens must hear, chase the facts, and hold the powerful to account.
c6_civics_ch15.finale: Free media isn't a bonus feature of democracy — it's the fourth pillar holding the roof up. No news means no one watching the watchers.
c6_civics_ch15.subtitle: What disappears when the news does?
c6_civics_ch15.role: editor of a busy newsroom for a day
c6_civics_ch15.intro: A flood in one state, a new law in Delhi, a scam in the municipal office — three stories, one deadline. What do the people most need to know?
c6_civics_ch15.goal: See media as a democratic tool that keeps citizens informed and governments honest.

discovery.question: Mina scrubs her own kitchen all afternoon — exhausting work! Next door, a cleaner is paid to do the exact same job. Same sweat, same sparkle — so why does only one count as 'economic'?
options: Money changed hands in one case — economic activity needs a transaction, not just effort
Mina's work is economic too, because hard work always counts
Neither is economic — cleaning is never real work
Both are economic — identical effort means identical category
discovery.answer: Money changed hands in one case — economic activity needs a transaction, not just effort
discovery.hook: Busy does not mean economic. The line isn't effort — it's exchange. Cook for family out of love: non-economic. Cook the same meal for pay: economic.

c6_civics_ch16.mission: Sort a whole neighbourhood's day — shopkeepers, parents, volunteers, delivery riders — into paid work and unpaid care, then defend every borderline call.
c6_civics_ch16.finale: Same task, different reason. When love does the work it's priceless; when payment does, it's economic. The rupee, not the sweat, draws the line.
c6_civics_ch16.subtitle: Same work, same sweat — so why is only one 'economic'?
c6_civics_ch16.role: a neighbourhood survey-taker sorting everyone's daily work
c6_civics_ch16.intro: A shopkeeper opens shutters, a parent packs tiffins, a volunteer plants trees. Which of today's activities earn money — and which earn something else?
c6_civics_ch16.goal: Draw the line between economic and non-economic activity — the transaction test.

discovery.question: A farmer grows perfect strawberries, but the road to the city is broken and there's no electricity for a fridge. The berries are excellent — so why will they still rot unsold?
options: Great products need roads, power and water to reach buyers — the 'backbone' beneath every business
The farmer should simply grow cheaper berries
Strawberries rot anyway — location and roads never matter
The only thing missing is a better picking machine
discovery.answer: Great products need roads, power and water to reach buyers — the 'backbone' beneath every business
discovery.hook: A factory's loom isn't infrastructure — the electricity feeding it is. Infrastructure is the invisible foundation under everything an economy builds on top.

c6_economics_ch07.mission: Rebuild a struggling village's foundation — choose where the first road, power line and school go — then watch which sectors spring to life.
c6_economics_ch07.finale: Before the shop, before the factory, before the harvest sells — somebody built a road and switched on a light. That's infrastructure: first in, always underneath.
c6_economics_ch07.subtitle: Why do perfect strawberries still rot on a broken road?
c6_economics_ch07.role: a planner deciding where a village's first road goes
c6_economics_ch07.intro: Ripe strawberries, a broken road, no fridge, no buyers. The village has everything except the invisible skeleton every economy stands on.
c6_economics_ch07.goal: Distinguish infrastructure (the foundation) from tools (the machines) — and see who benefits when a bridge appears.

discovery.question: A whole village hides savings under mattresses — 'the safest place there is!' Meanwhile a young woman can't find a loan to open her bakery. What connects the two problems?
options: Mattress money sleeps — inside a bank it would become loans for people like her
Nothing — mattresses and loans are completely unrelated
She should hunt for money under the mattresses too
The village simply needs more mattresses, not banks
discovery.answer: Mattress money sleeps — inside a bank it would become loans for people like her
discovery.hook: A bank isn't a vault that sits on cash — it's a bridge. Your deposit doesn't nap in a locker; it travels out as someone's bakery, then comes home with interest.

c6_economics_ch08.mission: Run the village bank for a year — accept deposits, choose who deserves the loans, and turn sleepy savings into new shops, farms and dreams.
c6_economics_ch08.finale: Deposits in, loans out — the bank is where saved money goes to work. Under the mattress it's safe; inside the bank it's alive.
c6_economics_ch08.subtitle: How does a 'community piggy bank' build bakeries?
c6_economics_ch08.role: village bank manager deciding who gets the next loan
c6_economics_ch08.intro: Farmers deposit their surplus; a baker needs a loan; a student wants her first account. Every rupee you take in can walk back out as someone's new beginning.
c6_economics_ch08.goal: See the bank as a bridge between savers and borrowers — not just a safe.

discovery.question: The cobbler has shoes and wants bread. The farmer has bread and wants a shirt. The weaver has a shirt and wants shoes. Nobody wants what's directly offered — why is this village stuck?
options: Barter needs a 'double coincidence of wants' — each side must want exactly what the other has
The villagers are stuck because their goods are too cheap
Barter only fails when people are unfriendly to each other
They're stuck because shoes are worth more than bread
discovery.answer: Barter needs a 'double coincidence of wants' — each side must want exactly what the other has
discovery.hook: Barter isn't just 'swapping stuff' — it's a lock that opens only when two wants match perfectly. Money is the master key that ended the waiting.

c6_economics_ch11.mission: Unstick a barter village — chain the trades so cobbler, farmer and weaver all get what they want — then invent the shortcut that makes it instant.
c6_economics_ch11.finale: Three people, three wants, zero trades — until money walks in. Money isn't just a thing to buy with; it's the agreement that lets everyone stop searching.
c6_economics_ch11.subtitle: Three villagers, three wants — and not a single trade
c6_economics_ch11.role: a trade negotiator in a village without money
c6_economics_ch11.intro: The cobbler wants bread, the farmer wants cloth, the weaver wants shoes — and nobody is offering the right swap. Welcome to the world's oldest trading puzzle.
c6_economics_ch11.goal: Feel why the double coincidence of wants made barter exhausting — and why money changed everything.

discovery.question: A shopkeeper insists, 'I run a market!' But for a whole month not a single customer walks in. His shop is real and his shelves are full — so is it still a market?
options: Not quite — a market needs buyers AND sellers meeting to exchange; an empty shop is only half a market
Yes — any building with goods for sale is automatically a market
No — markets must be outdoors, like vegetable stalls
Yes — the market exists as long as the rent is paid
discovery.answer: Not quite — a market needs buyers AND sellers meeting to exchange; an empty shop is only half a market
discovery.hook: A market isn't a place — it's a meeting. Buyer + seller + exchange can happen in a stall, a shop, or an app. No meeting, no market.

c6_economics_ch12.mission: Build a market from scratch — bring together people who want things and people who sell them — in a bazaar AND on a phone screen.
c6_economics_ch12.finale: Follow the pencil: your need met the shopkeeper's supply, and money carried the message. Wherever buyers and sellers meet — even online — that's the market.
c6_economics_ch12.subtitle: Is an empty shop still a market?
c6_economics_ch12.role: a market-maker matching buyers with sellers
c6_economics_ch12.intro: One shop, zero customers; one app, a million trades. Your job is to figure out what a market really is — and it isn't a building.
c6_economics_ch12.goal: Define a market by the exchange — buyer, seller, price — not by walls and stalls.

discovery.question: A teacher moves a story about a girl hearing a river speak from a quiet riverbank to a noisy, crowded classroom — and suddenly the whole story stops working. What broke it?
options: The quiet riverbank gave the girl the solitude to hear and reflect — the setting itself drives the events
Nothing broke — settings are just decoration and characters act the same anywhere
The classroom broke it only because the weather changed
The story broke because classrooms are always sad places in books
discovery.answer: The quiet riverbank gave the girl the solitude to hear and reflect — the setting itself drives the events
discovery.hook: Setting is not just scenery or weather. A quiet riverbank is a border between the familiar village and the unknown world — move the scene and the big moment can no longer happen.

c6_english_ch01.mission: Move the moment the river speaks into a crowded classroom, prove why the plot falls apart — then redesign one detail of the setting so the voice can still reach her.
c6_english_ch01.finale: The setting is the stage, and the plot is the performance. Change the stage, and the performance may never begin.

discovery.question: A story about a doctor who stops treating humans and takes language lessons from a parrot makes readers laugh — yet nobody in it tells a single joke. Where is the humour hiding?
options: In the absurd role-reversal — the expert doctor becomes a student of the parrot
In clever jokes the animals tell each other
In the animals doing silly tricks for no reason
It is not really funny — readers are just being polite
discovery.answer: In the absurd role-reversal — the expert doctor becomes a student of the parrot
discovery.hook: Humour is not only jokes. When characters act the opposite of what we expect — a doctor learning from an animal — the surprise itself is funny.

c6_english_ch02.mission: Track the plot from ordinary doctor to animal doctor and pin down exactly which flipped expectation makes each scene funny.
c6_english_ch02.finale: The funniest stories rarely tell jokes — they quietly flip the world upside down and let us laugh at ourselves.

discovery.question: A friend retells a story about a boy whose inventions keep failing — but skips the small early disasters and jumps straight to the biggest mess. The story falls flat. What went missing?
options: The build-up — each failed invention is bigger than the last, so the chain of disasters makes the finale funny
The character names — without them nothing makes sense
The jokes — every story needs jokes sprinkled in
Nothing — order never matters in a story
discovery.answer: The build-up — each failed invention is bigger than the last, so the chain of disasters makes the finale funny
discovery.hook: Sequence is not just a list of events. It is a chain of causes and effects — build, fail, react — that teaches readers to expect the next disaster.

c6_english_ch03.mission: Rebuild the scrambled order of the disasters of a young inventor and show why each mess must grow bigger than the one before it.
c6_english_ch03.finale: A story is beads on a string, not beads in a bag. The order of events is what turns mishaps into comedy.

discovery.question: A story about a boy near a jungle tunnel spends its first pages on his ordinary daily routine — nothing exciting happens at all. Why would a writer spend so much space on boring details?
options: Showing what is normal makes the sudden moment of danger feel far more surprising
To fill pages — long stories need padding
To describe the weather, which is the real point of the story
To introduce every villager before the plot begins
discovery.answer: Showing what is normal makes the sudden moment of danger feel far more surprising
discovery.hook: Plot is not everything a character does. It is the chain of important events that build toward a change — and a calm routine is the author loading the spring.

c6_english_ch04.mission: Map where a boy waits at a hot, still jungle tunnel each day, then mark the exact event that snaps his routine and pulls the story into danger.
c6_english_ch04.finale: Stillness before the storm is a trick of storytellers. The quieter the routine, the louder the surprise.

discovery.question: Two students write about visiting a war memorial. One lists facts like a textbook; the other begins Dear friend, guess what I saw today — and suddenly the whole class is listening. What did the letter do that the report could not?
options: It turned facts into feelings — a letter feels like a friend speaking directly to you
It used bigger words, which always impresses a class
It was longer, and longer writing always wins
It mentioned the memorial first, so it counted as research
discovery.answer: It turned facts into feelings — a letter feels like a friend speaking directly to you
discovery.hook: A letter is not a formal information document. Its greeting, personal voice, and warm sign-off make it a conversation — a bridge from the heart of the writer to the reader.

c6_english_ch05.mission: Take one cold fact about the war memorial and rewrite it as two sentences in a letter to a friend, adding the feeling the fact left behind.
c6_english_ch05.finale: Reports tell you what happened; letters tell you what it felt like. That is why a letter can make even stone walls speak.

discovery.question: In the same December week, a cousin in Kerala sends a beach selfie while a friend in Kashmir sends a photo of deep snow — both swear they are in India. Is one of them lying?
options: No — India is so vast it holds snowy mountains, deserts, beaches, and rainforests all at once
Yes — one country can only have one kind of landscape
Only if they live in different states — state borders decide the land
Yes — snow and beaches cannot exist in the same season
discovery.answer: No — India is so vast it holds snowy mountains, deserts, beaches, and rainforests all at once
discovery.hook: Geographical diversity is about the land itself — mountains, deserts, coasts, forests — not the state lines drawn on a political map. The size and location of India make the variety possible.

c6_geography_ch01.mission: Plan a road trip from the Himalayas to Kerala and mark the four totally different landscapes you cross — then explain why one country can hold them all.
c6_geography_ch01.finale: India is not one landscape but a collection of many, stitched together by size and location. One ticket, many worlds.

discovery.question: A tourist spends two rainy days in a desert town and announces that the desert has a rainy climate now. What did they get wrong?
options: Two rainy days are just weather — climate is the average pattern measured over 30 years or more
Nothing — rain is rain, wherever it falls
They got it wrong because deserts can never have rain at all
They should have said season instead of climate
discovery.answer: Two rainy days are just weather — climate is the average pattern measured over 30 years or more
discovery.hook: Weather is a snapshot of today; climate is the album of many years. One unusual day never rewrites the personality of a place.

c6_geography_ch02.mission: Sort a pile of statements — It is hot today, This region is usually dry, Storm tonight — into weather and climate, and defend each call using the time factor.
c6_geography_ch02.finale: Check the sky for weather; check the decades for climate. The umbrella question and the woolen question are answered by two different clocks.

discovery.question: It is December. Srinagar needs heavy woolens, Chennai needs light cotton — and a mountaintop sitting near the equator is still freezing. What invisible recipe is setting each temperature?
options: Latitude, altitude, and distance from the sea mix together to cook the climate of each place
Luck — some places are just born cold
Only the month decides — same month should mean same temperature
Buildings — cities make their own climate from concrete
discovery.answer: Latitude, altitude, and distance from the sea mix together to cook the climate of each place
discovery.hook: Climate is not random and not decided by one thing. Where a place sits on the globe, how high it rises, and how near the sea it is — each factor adjusts the temperature like a dial.

c6_geography_ch03.mission: Given three mystery cities — one near the equator, one on a high peak, one far inland — predict which is hottest, coldest, and most extreme, then explain each using the climate factors.
c6_geography_ch03.finale: Every place has a climate recipe: a pinch of latitude, a height of altitude, a splash of sea. Learn the recipe and you can predict a place before you ever visit.

discovery.question: For thousands of years people wandered to find food — then around 7000 BCE near the Indus, someone planted wheat and barley and everything changed. How did a seed end the wandering and eventually build cities?
options: Farming near rivers gave a steady food supply, so people settled, stored surplus, and villages grew into cities
People got tired of walking and simply stopped
Rivers pushed people into cities by flooding the forests
Cities appeared first, and farming was invented inside them
discovery.answer: Farming near rivers gave a steady food supply, so people settled, stored surplus, and villages grew into cities
discovery.hook: Farming did not begin everywhere at once. Wheat and barley started in the northwest around 7000 BCE; rice in the Ganga region came later, around 5000 BCE — agriculture spread in stages.

c6_geography_ch04.mission: Follow a seed from a riverbank in the northwest to a stored surplus, and trace how that surplus frees some people to build, craft, and run a city.
c6_geography_ch04.finale: A city is built on stored grain. Once food could stay in one place, so could people — and villages grew into civilisation.

discovery.question: A classmate claims every neighbour of India shares a land border with it. Which two neighbours quietly prove them wrong — and why?
options: Sri Lanka and the Maldives — they sit across the ocean with water, not land, between them and India
China and Nepal — they are separated by tall mountains
Pakistan and Bangladesh — their borders were drawn later
Bhutan and Myanmar — they are too small to touch India
discovery.answer: Sri Lanka and the Maldives — they sit across the ocean with water, not land, between them and India
discovery.hook: Neighbours come in two kinds: land neighbours that share a border and island neighbours across the sea. Direction matters too — Pakistan to the west, Myanmar to the east, China and Nepal to the north.

c6_geography_ch05.mission: Stand at the centre of India and turn like a compass — name the neighbour in each direction and mark which two you can only reach by crossing water.
c6_geography_ch05.finale: India has seven land neighbours and two island ones. Know the direction of each, and the map of South Asia falls into place.

discovery.question: A group that follows herds and picks wild berries moves camp every season. Why could they never build a city — while a farming village slowly could?
options: Farming produced surplus food, so people could stay put, grow in number, and free some hands for pottery and tools
Wanderers were too lazy to build walls
Cities only appear where gold is found
Herds of animals knocked down every building
discovery.answer: Farming produced surplus food, so people could stay put, grow in number, and free some hands for pottery and tools
discovery.hook: Nobody woke up one morning and decided to build a city. Small farming villages swelled over thousands of years as surplus food let some people stop farming and start specializing.

c6_history_ch04.mission: Trace a seed of grain into a stored surplus, then show how that surplus turns a quiet village into a bustling early city with potters, traders, and builders.
c6_history_ch04.finale: A city is a village that stopped wandering. Feed more people than can farm, and the rest will build the future.

discovery.question: Picture a school where every student is an independent king making their own rules. Around 321 BCE, Chandragupta Maurya and his advisor Chanakya did something like turning all those rulers into one team. How?
options: Through conquest and diplomacy — small mahajanapadas were merged under a single central authority
By asking nicely once and hoping for the best
By building a giant wall around each kingdom
By moving everyone to a new empty land
discovery.answer: Through conquest and diplomacy — small mahajanapadas were merged under a single central authority
discovery.hook: The empire did not rise in an empty land. The subcontinent was already full of organized mahajanapadas — Chandragupta united pieces that already existed rather than starting from scratch.

c6_history_ch05.mission: Take charge beside Chandragupta and Chanakya — decide when to fight and when to make an alliance as you fold rival mahajanapadas into one empire.
c6_history_ch05.finale: An empire is a puzzle solved with both sword and treaty. Many small kingdoms became one power for the first time.

discovery.question: Your school today looks nothing like the one your grandparents attended. Historians say all of India changed the same way around 700 CE — but what actually changed enough to start a whole new period?
options: Old empires collapsed and regional kingdoms, new faiths, new art, and new ways of ruling took their place
A comet hit India and restarted the calendar
Everyone simply agreed to rename the era
Nothing changed — historians just needed a label
discovery.answer: Old empires collapsed and regional kingdoms, new faiths, new art, and new ways of ruling took their place
discovery.hook: Medieval does not mean primitive stone-age times. The period from about 700 to 1700 CE is a bridge — the era when the culture, language, and art we recognize today began to form.

c6_history_ch06.mission: Act as a historian deciding whether a new period has begun — check if rulers, religions, buildings, and daily life all shifted, then stamp 700 CE as your starting line.
c6_history_ch06.finale: Periods are not random labels on a timeline. When power, prayer, and painting all transform together, history turns a page.

discovery.question: In 1206 a man who had once been enslaved declared himself the independent ruler of Delhi — and the empire he began lasted 320 years. How does a former slave become a Sultan?
options: Qutbuddin Aibak was a trusted general of Muhammad of Ghur who took charge after his leader died
He won a wrestling match against the old king
He was secretly a prince the whole time
The people of Delhi elected him in a vote
discovery.answer: Qutbuddin Aibak was a trusted general of Muhammad of Ghur who took charge after his leader died
discovery.hook: Aibak did not conquer India alone from the start — he served another ruler first and declared independence only in 1206. And the Sultanate was not one family: five successive dynasties held the throne.

c6_history_ch07.mission: Stand beside Aibak at the moment of decision in 1206 — weigh the risk of declaring independence, then follow the baton of power through the dynasties that ruled until 1526.
c6_history_ch07.finale: Skill and loyalty could outrank royal birth. One act of independence in 1206 opened three centuries of Sultanate rule.

discovery.question: Two brothers in 1336 name their brand-new capital Vijayanagara — city of victory — and today its stone chariot still stands at Hampi. What were Harihara and Bukka really announcing?
options: A kingdom built to stand strong against challenges — a statement of victory carved into a city name
That they had already conquered the whole world
That the city was a gift from a neighbouring king
That victory parades would be held every week
discovery.answer: A kingdom built to stand strong against challenges — a statement of victory carved into a city name
discovery.hook: Vijayanagara was not the only kingdom in India then. Many regional powers existed side by side — the empire, peaking under Krishnadevaraya, was one brilliant piece of a diverse medieval map.

c6_history_ch08.mission: Walk the ruins of Hampi — from the Virupaksha temple to the stone chariot — and rebuild the story of two brothers whose city of victory ruled the south for three centuries.
c6_history_ch08.finale: Name a city victory and you set its destiny. For over 300 years, Vijayanagara lived up to its name.

discovery.question: In 1526, a traveler from Central Asia wins a single battle at Panipat — and the map of India changes for centuries. How could one morning do all that?
options: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, ending the dominance of the Delhi Sultanate and planting the Mughal Empire
He found a magic crown lying on the battlefield
The Delhi army simply went home that day
He bought the throne of Delhi with trade goods
discovery.answer: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, ending the dominance of the Delhi Sultanate and planting the Mughal Empire
discovery.hook: Babur was not already an Indian king taking over. He was an outsider who saw India as a land of opportunity and had to fight his way in — the empire began with a battlefield, not a birthright.

c6_history_ch09.mission: Relive the First Battle of Panipat — weigh what Babur risked, what Ibrahim Lodi lost, and what a defeat would have done to the dream of a Mughal Empire.
c6_history_ch09.finale: One battle can end an era and begin another. Panipat, 1526 — the day the Sultanate closed and the Mughal age opened.

discovery.question: In the 1600s the English built a factory at Surat — but there were no machines, no chimneys, no workers on assembly lines. So what exactly was this factory?
options: A warehouse and trading post where merchants stored goods before shipping them home
A secret school for training sailors
A fortress built to invade the Mughal capital
A workshop that wove cloth for local markets
discovery.answer: A warehouse and trading post where merchants stored goods before shipping them home
discovery.hook: The British were not the first or the only Europeans in India. Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498, the Portuguese claimed Goa, and the Dutch came too — a factory then meant storage and trade, not industry.

c6_history_ch10.mission: Map the arrivals — place Vasco da Gama in 1498, the Portuguese base at Goa, and the English post at Surat — and order who anchored on the coast of India first.
c6_history_ch10.finale: First a warehouse on a coast, then an empire. The Europeans did not just visit India — they unpacked and stayed.

discovery.question: The British built railways and spread newspapers to run India more easily — yet those very tools helped Indians unite against British rule. How did the tools backfire?
options: Trains and newspapers connected people across regions, who discovered they shared the same problems and the same hopes
Indians sabotaged the trains to send a message
Newspapers printed secret codes only Indians could read
The British handed out free tickets to protests
discovery.answer: Trains and newspapers connected people across regions, who discovered they shared the same problems and the same hopes
discovery.hook: Nationalism did not appear overnight, and not everyone agreed from day one. It grew gradually — and the early Congress, founded in Bombay in 1885, was moderate, asking for fair treatment within the system.

c6_history_ch11.mission: Follow a newspaper and a railway ticket across 1880s India — collect the shared complaints they carry — and deliver them to the first meeting of the Congress in Bombay.
c6_history_ch11.finale: A nation is born when strangers discover they share a struggle. Trains carried the people; newspapers carried the idea.

discovery.question: Fifty friends start a club with no rules and argue about everything. In 1947, India was that club — with hundreds of millions of members. What stopped the chaos?
options: The Constituent Assembly wrote a Constitution — a rulebook for government and the rights of every citizen
One leader wrote all the rules alone in a single night
The old British laws were kept forever unchanged
Each region made its own private rules with no agreement
discovery.answer: The Constituent Assembly wrote a Constitution — a rulebook for government and the rights of every citizen
discovery.hook: The Constitution was not written by one person. Nearly 299 members from every region debated together — Dr B R Ambedkar led the Drafting Committee, but the Assembly spoke for the whole nation.

c6_history_ch12.mission: Sit in the Constituent Assembly — argue for rules that protect every citizen — and help the Drafting Committee turn hundreds of voices into one rulebook for India.
c6_history_ch12.finale: A country this diverse runs on agreed rules, not on one voice. The Constitution is the debate of a whole nation, written down.

discovery.question: A stadium holds thousands of cheering people and the organizer announces the crowd size minutes after the gates close. Nobody counted heads one by one — so how did they get a number?
options: They counted a small sample area, estimated the rest, and got a close-enough total fast
They made up a random big number
They weighed the stadium before and after
They asked every person to raise a hand at once
discovery.answer: They counted a small sample area, estimated the rest, and got a close-enough total fast
discovery.hook: Estimation is not random guessing. It is a logical shortcut — when exact counting is slow or impossible, a smart about-value is enough to plan with.

c6_math_ch01.mission: Face a crowd too big to count — pick a sample patch, scale it up, and defend your estimated total against someone demanding an exact count.
c6_math_ch01.finale: Numbers are tools, not just symbols — they tell you if you have enough money, enough time, and roughly how many people showed up.

discovery.question: Two cities report their temperatures: one is -5 degrees, the other -2. A classmate says the -5 city is warmer because 5 is bigger than 2. Where did they slip?
options: The minus sign flips the rule — -5 is further below zero, so that city is colder
Nowhere — 5 really is bigger than 2
Both cities are equally cold because both are negative
-5 is warmer only at night
discovery.answer: The minus sign flips the rule — -5 is further below zero, so that city is colder
discovery.hook: On the negative side of the number line, bigger digits mean smaller values. -10 is less than -1 because it sits further from zero — the sign changes everything.

c6_math_ch02.mission: Ride an elevator that goes below ground — label the basement floors with negative numbers, then decide which of two frosty cities is colder.
c6_math_ch02.finale: Zero is the border, not a team member. Negative numbers are not debts to fear — they are just positions on the other side.

discovery.question: At a party your friend crows that they scored 1/8 of the cake while you only got 1/4. Should you feel cheated?
options: No — 1/4 is a bigger piece, because cutting into fewer equal parts makes each part larger
Yes — 8 is bigger than 4, so 1/8 must be more cake
You got the same — all fractions of a cake are equal
Only if the cake was square instead of round
discovery.answer: No — 1/4 is a bigger piece, because cutting into fewer equal parts makes each part larger
discovery.hook: A bigger denominator means a smaller share, not a bigger one. And if the pieces are not equal in size, it is not a fraction at all — fair sharing is the whole point.

c6_math_ch03.mission: Split a paratha, a chocolate bar, and a kilo of apples into fair shares — write each share as a fraction and prove the pieces are truly equal.
c6_math_ch03.finale: A fraction is a promise: the bottom number counts the equal pieces, the top counts yours. Break the equality and the promise breaks too.

discovery.question: A scoreboard shows two jumps: 0.4 metres and 0.25 metres. A classmate insists 0.25 is the longer jump because 25 is bigger than 4. Settle the argument.
options: 0.4 wins — it means 40 hundredths, while 0.25 is only 25 hundredths
0.25 wins — more digits after the point always means a bigger number
They tie — both are less than one so both are equal
0.4 wins only because it was written first
discovery.answer: 0.4 wins — it means 40 hundredths, while 0.25 is only 25 hundredths
discovery.hook: Digits after the decimal point are not whole numbers — they are tenths and hundredths. Read them as fractions of one, and the mystery of 0.4 beating 0.25 disappears.

c6_math_ch04.mission: Turn a ruler into a decimal machine — convert millimetres into tenths of a centimetre, then rank three jumps written as decimals.
c6_math_ch04.finale: The decimal point is a divider: wholes on the left, pieces of one on the right. Once you know the places, decimals stop being scary.

discovery.question: A rickshaw driver charges 20 rupees for the ride plus 5 rupees for every kilometre. During your trip, which part of the fare keeps changing — and which part never budges?
options: The 5-per-kilometre part grows with distance; the flat 20 stays fixed
Both parts change every minute
The 20 changes with distance; the 5 stays fixed
Nothing changes — the fare is decided before you sit
discovery.answer: The 5-per-kilometre part grows with distance; the flat 20 stays fixed
discovery.hook: In 20 + 5k, the letter k is the variable — it stands for whatever distance you travel. The 5 and the 20 are constants. Even the number glued to a letter, like 5 in 5k, is still a constant.

c6_math_ch05.mission: Build the fare formula 20 + 5k yourself — label the variable and the constants, then predict the cost of a 4 km ride and a 10 km ride.
c6_math_ch05.finale: Algebra begins with one question: what changes and what does not? Letters carry the changing part; numbers hold the fixed part.

discovery.question: One recipe card says mix 2 cups of sugar for every 6 cups of water. Another says 1 to 3. Your cousin insists the second drink is weaker. Are they right?
options: No — 2:6 simplifies to 1:3, so both drinks have exactly the same sweetness
Yes — smaller numbers always mean a weaker mix
Yes — the second recipe forgot half the sugar
No — the first drink is actually weaker
discovery.answer: No — 2:6 simplifies to 1:3, so both drinks have exactly the same sweetness
discovery.hook: A ratio is a relationship, not a shopping list — it simplifies like a fraction. But order matters (2 sugar to 6 water is not 6 to 2), and the units must match before you compare.

c6_math_ch06.mission: Rescue a recipe mix-up — rewrite 2:6 in simplest form, then catch the error when someone compares 2 metres of ribbon to 50 centimetres of lace as 2:50.
c6_math_ch06.finale: Two different-looking ratios can hide the same relationship. Simplify first, match the units, and the truth pours out.

discovery.question: You mark two dots on a page and a friend claims they can draw many different straight lines through both dots. Can they?
options: No — exactly one straight line passes through two given points
Yes — as many lines as there are colours of pen
Yes — but only if the dots are close together
No — no line can pass through two points at once
discovery.answer: No — exactly one straight line passes through two given points
discovery.hook: A line does not stop at the edge of your paper — the arrows mean it runs forever. A line segment, with its two endpoint dots, is the stopped, measurable piece of that endless line.

c6_math_ch07.mission: Draw a dot, connect two points into a segment, then stretch it past the page in both directions — and name each figure correctly as it transforms.
c6_math_ch07.finale: Two points fix one line forever. Points are locations, segments are journeys with ends, and lines are journeys that never end.

discovery.question: A gardener orders fencing for a 10 metre by 5 metre garden by adding 10 + 5 = 15 metres. When the wire arrives, half the garden stands open. What did they forget?
options: A rectangle has four sides — the real boundary is 10 + 5 + 10 + 5 = 30 metres
Nothing — 15 metres is the correct perimeter
They forgot to multiply by the height of the fence
They should have measured the area inside instead
discovery.answer: A rectangle has four sides — the real boundary is 10 + 5 + 10 + 5 = 30 metres
discovery.hook: Perimeter is the full walk around the edge, not just the numbers printed in the question. Bonus twist: two different rectangles, like 6 by 2 and 5 by 3, can share the same perimeter.

c6_math_ch08.mission: Walk the boundary of a garden, a triangle, and a notebook — total every side — then work backwards to find a missing side when only the perimeter is known.
c6_math_ch08.finale: Perimeter answers one question only: how far is the trip around the outside? Trace every edge, and no side gets left behind.

discovery.question: You asked 40 classmates their favourite fruit and now hold a messy list of words. Why does grouping it into a tally table suddenly reveal the winner?
options: The table counts how often each answer appears, so the most popular choice is visible at a glance
Tables make handwriting neater, which reveals the answer
The tallest column always belongs to your favourite fruit
Grouping deletes the unpopular answers
discovery.answer: The table counts how often each answer appears, so the most popular choice is visible at a glance
discovery.hook: Tally marks are the counting tool; frequency is the final count. And tallies bundle in fives — a diagonal stroke across four bars — so big counts can be read in one look.

c6_math_ch09.mission: Run a real survey at the school gate — set categories, mark one tally per observation, bundle every five — then read the table to crown the most common choice.
c6_math_ch09.finale: Raw data is noise; a frequency table is the pattern hiding inside it. Organize first, and the answer announces itself.

discovery.question: You fold paper, cut half a heart, and open a perfect mirror-image shape. But a scalene triangle sliced into two equal-area pieces is not symmetric. Why does equal size fail the test?
options: Symmetry needs mirror-image halves that fold exactly onto each other — equal area alone is not enough
Because triangles can never be symmetric
Because the cut was not made with scissors
Equal size always proves symmetry — the triangle counts
discovery.answer: Symmetry needs mirror-image halves that fold exactly onto each other — equal area alone is not enough
discovery.hook: The line of symmetry is a mirror, not a measuring tape. A butterfly proves it — and an equilateral triangle proves a shape can have not one but three such mirror lines.

c6_math_ch10.mission: Hunt for mirror lines — fold a rectangle to find its two lines of symmetry, check the letter A, then draw a shape with at least two of your own.
c6_math_ch10.finale: Symmetry is a folding promise: one side must land exactly on the other. If the mirror completes the picture, the line is true.

discovery.question: Two students argue over whose angle is bigger — one drew a small opening with very long arms, the other a wide opening with tiny arms. Who actually wins?
options: The wide opening — an angle is the turn at the vertex, and arm length does not matter
The long arms — longer lines always mean a bigger angle
They tie — every drawn angle is the same size
Neither — angles cannot be compared without colours
discovery.answer: The wide opening — an angle is the turn at the vertex, and arm length does not matter
discovery.hook: Construction means replacing guessing with measuring — ruler for straight lines, compass for curves, protractor centred on the vertex. And you need not start at zero: drawing from the 1 cm mark to the 6 cm mark still gives exactly 5 cm.

c6_math_ch11.mission: Open the geometry box — pick the right tool for each task — and construct a 5 cm segment and an exact angle, placing the protractor centre dead on the vertex.
c6_math_ch11.finale: A freehand sketch hopes to be right; a construction knows it is right. The tools turn looking close into measuring exactly.

discovery.question: A shopkeeper sells candle packs of 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 — and every pack grows by a bigger jump than the last. How many candles are in the next pack?
options: 21 — the gaps grow as +2, +3, +4, +5, so the next gap is +6
20 — the pattern adds 5 every time
16 — just add 1 to the last number
18 — the gaps repeat +3 forever
discovery.answer: 21 — the gaps grow as +2, +3, +4, +5, so the next gap is +6
discovery.hook: Not every pattern adds the same number. Check the gaps between the gaps — 2, 4, 6, 8 adds while 2, 4, 8, 16 multiplies, and triangular numbers grow by bigger and bigger steps.

c6_math_ch12.mission: Crack the hidden rule in three sequences — one adding, one squaring, one triangle-building — then predict the next three terms of each without guessing.
c6_math_ch12.finale: Every pattern has a rule doing quiet work between the numbers. Find the rule, and the future of the sequence is yours.

discovery.question: A flashlight suddenly dies. One friend tosses it in the bin; another guesses the battery is dead, swaps in a fresh one, and it lights up. Only one of them did science — who, and why?
options: The second friend — they observed the problem, made a guess, and tested it
The first friend — deciding it was broken was a fast scientific conclusion
Both — science is whatever happens around machines
Neither — real science needs a lab coat and test tubes
discovery.answer: The second friend — they observed the problem, made a guess, and tested it
discovery.hook: Science is not a finished book of facts to memorize. It is a detective loop — observe, question, guess, test — and a careful experiment can even overturn what a textbook says.

c6_physics_ch01.mission: A wilting plant and a suspicious bouncing ball both need a detective — run the full observe-question-guess-test loop on each and record your evidence.
c6_physics_ch01.finale: Science is a verb, not a shelf of facts. Anyone who asks why and then tests the answer is already doing it.

discovery.question: You spend twenty minutes watching an ant haul a crumb across the garden, noting its path and speed. Your sibling laughs that you are wasting time. Who is right?
options: You are — tracking the ant, recording what it does, and asking why is real scientific data collection
Your sibling — science only counts inside a laboratory
Neither — watching insects is just a hobby
You are — but only because ants are famous
discovery.answer: You are — tracking the ant, recording what it does, and asking why is real scientific data collection
discovery.hook: Nature is the oldest laboratory in the world. Long before buildings and equipment existed, humans survived by noticing patterns — and the most important scientific tool is still careful observation, not a microscope.

c6_physics_ch02.mission: Take a nature walk as a field scientist — pick one small mystery like a line of ants or a drying puddle, form a testable question, and record what changes over time.
c6_physics_ch02.finale: The difference between looking and observing is a notebook. Step outside, ask what is happening here, and the backyard becomes a lab.

discovery.question: A torch has a fresh battery inside and the switch is OFF. Where did all the electricity go — and why does sliding the switch bring the bulb to life?
options: The switch leaves a gap in the loop; closing it completes the path so electricity can flow from the battery, through the bulb, and back
The electricity fell asleep and the switch wakes it up
The bulb drinks the electricity only when switched on
The switch pushes stored light out of the battery
discovery.answer: The switch leaves a gap in the loop; closing it completes the path so electricity can flow from the battery, through the bulb, and back
discovery.hook: A circuit is a loop, like a circular train track — any gap stops the train. Electricity is not used up by the bulb; it leaves the battery, lights the bulb, and returns home.

c6_physics_ch03.mission: Build a torch in your head — place battery, bulb, and switch — then diagnose three failures: switch OFF, dead battery, and fused bulb.
c6_physics_ch03.finale: No loop, no light. A switch is just a drawbridge for electricity — down means flow, up means stop.

discovery.question: You hold an ice cube and your friend announces that cold is flowing into your hand. What is actually moving — and in which direction?
options: Heat flows out of your warm hand into the ice — cold is just the absence of heat, not a thing that travels
Cold flows from the ice into your hand, exactly as your friend said
Nothing moves — the feeling is imaginary
Heat and cold swap places and trade spots
discovery.answer: Heat flows out of your warm hand into the ice — cold is just the absence of heat, not a thing that travels
discovery.hook: Heat is energy that always runs downhill from hot to cold until both match. It moves three ways — through solids by conduction, through air and water by convection, and through empty space by radiation.

c6_physics_ch07.mission: Track three heat journeys — a spoon in hot tea, warm air rising off a heater, and sunlight crossing space — and name which mode of transfer each one uses.
c6_physics_ch07.finale: There is no such thing as a flow of cold. Every chill you feel is heat leaving you for somewhere cooler.

discovery.question: A stick in the ground tells perfect time all sunny afternoon — its shadow crawling like a clock hand. But at midnight it is completely useless. Why?
options: A sundial needs sunlight to cast a shadow — and the shadow moves only because the sun appears to shift as Earth rotates
The stick gets tired and stops working at night
Moonlight is too weak to ever make any shadow
Sundials need to be wound up every evening
discovery.answer: A sundial needs sunlight to cast a shadow — and the shadow moves only because the sun appears to shift as Earth rotates
discovery.hook: The stick never moves — Earth does. The sun only appears to travel across the sky because our planet spins, and it is that shifting light angle that drags the shadow around the dial.

c6_physics_ch08.mission: Plant a stick in open ground, mark its shadow tip with a pebble every hour, and figure out why a cloudy day defeats your homemade clock.
c6_physics_ch08.finale: The first clock was a shadow. It worked beautifully — as long as the biggest light in the sky was switched on.

discovery.question: On a bright moonlit night, a friend calls the Moon a natural source of light, just like the Sun. Are they right?
options: No — the Moon only bounces sunlight back to us; a true source makes its own light, like the Sun, stars, or a firefly
Yes — anything glowing in the night sky counts as a source
Yes — moonlight is made inside the Moon
No — the Moon is actually an artificial satellite
discovery.answer: No — the Moon only bounces sunlight back to us; a true source makes its own light, like the Sun, stars, or a firefly
discovery.hook: Glowing is not the same as producing. Mirrors and the Moon reflect light made elsewhere — while a tiny firefly, glowing by its own chemistry, is a genuine natural source. Artificial sources are the ones humans built, like bulbs and candles.

c6_physics_ch11.mission: Sort a jumble of glowing things — Sun, moon, mirror, firefly, candle, phone screen — into emitters, reflectors, natural, and artificial, and defend each label.
c6_physics_ch11.finale: Ask one question of any bright thing: did it make this light, or borrow it? That single test separates every source from every mirror.

discovery.question: Your uncle insists the Sun rises because it travels across the sky every day, just like a bus crossing town. What is actually moving?
options: We are — Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours, carrying us into sunlight and back out
The Sun — it really does circle the Earth daily
The clouds — they drag the Sun across the sky
Nothing moves — light simply fades and returns
discovery.answer: We are — Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours, carrying us into sunlight and back out
discovery.hook: Day and night exist because Earth is a spinning sphere — sunlight can only ever light one half at a time. The sun seems to cross the sky for the same reason a lamp seems to spin when you turn in a circle: the observer is the one moving.

c6_physics_ch12.mission: Shine a flashlight on a ball in a dark room, spin the ball slowly, and show why one side lives in day while the other lives in night — then explain what happens if the spinning stops.
c6_physics_ch12.finale: The Sun does not rise — we roll toward it. Every sunrise is just your spot on Earth turning back into the light.

discovery.question: In one family album: a baby, a schoolchild, a teenager who shot up centimetres in a year, a parent, and a grandparent whose body is slowly slowing down. What invisible programme flips each person from one chapter to the next?
options: Chemical messengers called hormones, working with the genetic blueprint, drive the body through predictable stages
Birthdays alone — age numbers force the body to change
Food quantity — eating more makes you enter the next stage
Random chance — nobody really knows why bodies change
discovery.answer: Chemical messengers called hormones, working with the genetic blueprint, drive the body through predictable stages
discovery.hook: Adolescence is a bridge, not an island — it carries the body from childhood to adulthood through one of the fastest growth phases after infancy. And a missing signal matters: too little growth hormone from the pituitary can stunt the journey.

c7_bio_ch01.mission: Line up the five human life stages in order, then trace how hormones carry a body across the bridge of adolescence into adulthood.
c7_bio_ch01.finale: Every body walks the same road — infancy to old age — but hormones decide the speed of each step. Growing up is chemistry on a schedule.

discovery.question: A stray dog gulps down spoiled food crawling with bacteria. Hours later it is fine — and it kept breathing even on a day it found no food at all. Which hidden teamwork saved it?
options: Nutrition, respiration, and excretion work as one network — digestion takes in fuel, breathing releases its energy, and excretion removes the toxic leftovers
The dog just has a lucky stomach
Breathing stops whenever eating stops, so the dog was not really hungry
The food simply disappeared once swallowed
discovery.answer: Nutrition, respiration, and excretion work as one network — digestion takes in fuel, breathing releases its energy, and excretion removes the toxic leftovers
discovery.hook: No life process works alone — and two wastes are not the same. Undigested food leaving the gut is egestion, but chemical waste made inside cells, like urea filtered by the kidneys, is true excretion.

c7_bio_ch02.mission: Follow a glass of milk through a calf — chart how nutrition delivers it, respiration burns it with oxygen, and excretion throws out what cells cannot use.
c7_bio_ch02.finale: Your body is a three-way relay: food in, energy out, waste gone. Drop any runner and the whole race is lost.

discovery.question: A money plant thrives on a sunny balcony, but its twin in a dark cupboard turns pale and stops growing — even with plenty of water and the richest soil. What did the cupboard steal?
options: Sunlight — without it the plant cannot make its own food, no matter how much water and soil it has
Nothing — the plant was just sleeping
Fresh air only — plants suffocate in cupboards
Fertilizer — dark rooms drain nutrients
discovery.answer: Sunlight — without it the plant cannot make its own food, no matter how much water and soil it has
discovery.hook: Plants do not eat soil. Weigh a pot before planting and months later — the soil barely shrinks. Soil lends minerals and an anchor; sunlight powers the kitchen where the plant actually cooks its food.

c7_bio_ch03.mission: Set up a fair test with two identical seedlings — one in light, one in darkness, same water and soil — and read the pale leaves to prove which factor is missing.
c7_bio_ch03.finale: Sunlight is the stove, water the delivery truck, soil the pantry shelf. Remove the stove and the finest pantry still serves nothing.

discovery.question: A shiny grey pencil lead gets stamped metal for its shine, while an old unpolished gold bangle gets stamped non-metal for looking dull. What single test would sort them honestly?
options: Strike them — metals like iron flatten under a hammer while non-metals like coal shatter to powder
Weigh them — metals are always heavier
Taste them — metals taste salty
Freeze them — only metals survive cold
discovery.answer: Strike them — metals like iron flatten under a hammer while non-metals like coal shatter to powder
discovery.hook: Shine lies — graphite and iodine crystals gleam yet are non-metals. And the rules have rebels: mercury is a metal that flows liquid at room temperature, while bromine is a liquid non-metal.

c7_chem_ch01.mission: Raid a kitchen for suspects — iron spoon, chalk, copper wire, coal — and run the shine test, the hammer test, and the wiring test to file each under metal or non-metal.
c7_chem_ch01.finale: Never judge an element by its glitter. Bend it, strike it, run a current through it — behaviour reveals what appearance hides.

discovery.question: In one busy morning, sugar vanishes into tea, milk sours into curd, and paper burns to ash. All three look dramatic — but only some can never be undone. What is the real test?
options: Ask if a new substance was born — dissolved sugar can be recovered by evaporation, but curd and ash can never turn back
Ask how big the change looks — dramatic changes are always chemical
Ask if heat was involved — heat always means chemical
Ask if it happened in a kitchen — kitchen changes are reversible
discovery.answer: Ask if a new substance was born — dissolved sugar can be recovered by evaporation, but curd and ash can never turn back
discovery.hook: Looks deceive. Tearing paper, boiling water, and dissolving salt feel drastic but stay physical — the same stuff in a new form. Even heat is no proof: melting ice absorbs heat yet stays water.

c7_chem_ch02.mission: Run a home change-detective log — boiling water, a ripening banana, dissolved salt, a cooked egg — and label each physical or chemical using only evidence you can see.
c7_chem_ch02.finale: Every change answers to one question: is the original still hiding inside? If you can win it back, nothing new was truly born.

discovery.question: A school with no timetable, no rules, and no teachers descends into chaos within minutes. Yet a country of over a billion people keeps its trains, hospitals, and courts running even when leaders change. Who is really keeping it going?
options: The government — a permanent system of institutions, courts, and civil services, not just the politicians currently in power
The Prime Minister personally runs every service
Citizens manage everything alone with no coordination
Private companies run all public services for free
discovery.answer: The government — a permanent system of institutions, courts, and civil services, not just the politicians currently in power
discovery.hook: Government is not the face on the news — ministers come and go with elections, but the railways, hospitals, police, and courts keep running. Lawmaking, enforcing, and dispute-settling are split across separate branches so no single hand holds all power.

c7_civ_ch01.mission: A new island of 500 people needs governing by tonight — list the three functions its government must perform first, and defend why individuals cannot handle them alone.
c7_civ_ch01.finale: Rules do not shrink freedom — they guard it. Government exists so that the strong cannot simply do whatever they want to the weak.

discovery.question: Parliament passes a law that clashes head-on with the Constitution — say, banning a freedom the Constitution guarantees. In this collision, which document wins, and who calls it?
options: The Constitution wins — it is the supreme law, and the courts strike down any ordinary law that violates it
Parliament wins — the newest law always overrules older documents
Nobody wins — both laws apply at the same time
The Prime Minister decides which one counts
discovery.answer: The Constitution wins — it is the supreme law, and the courts strike down any ordinary law that violates it
discovery.hook: The Constitution is not a history book frozen in 1950 — it is the living rulebook that even the rulers must obey. Ordinary laws change with a simple vote; the Constitution demands a much harder special process, so nobody can rewrite the game mid-play.

c7_civ_ch02.mission: Draft a mini-constitution for your school — write one clause that stops any single council member from holding absolute power, then test it against a misuse scenario.
c7_civ_ch02.finale: At the top of the legal pyramid sits one document everyone — citizen and minister alike — must answer to. That is what supreme really means.

discovery.question: A new Prime Minister takes the oath and headlines scream about a new government. But has India — the country — actually changed? What stays standing when a government is voted out?
options: The state stays — its territory, people, sovereignty, courts, and civil services are permanent; only the temporary government changed
The whole state is recreated with every election
The borders redraw themselves each time leaders change
Nothing stays — every election builds a new country
discovery.answer: The state stays — its territory, people, sovereignty, courts, and civil services are permanent; only the temporary government changed
discovery.hook: State and government are not the same word. The state is the school building, playground, and students — the government is just this year's elected council running it. Citizens may criticise and vote out a government while still owing allegiance to the state.

c7_civ_ch03.mission: A flood hits and relief must roll — assign the roles: who sets policy and releases funds, and who delivers relief on the ground and stays even after the next election.
c7_civ_ch03.finale: Governments are hired and fired; the state endures. Knowing which is which is the first lesson of a thinking citizen.

discovery.question: You stand in a village haat holding a basket of wheat, desperate for sandals — and money does not exist. Before you can walk home in new shoes, what lucky match must happen?
options: You must find a cobbler who both has spare sandals and wants your wheat — a double match of wants, negotiated on the spot
You just hand over wheat and take any sandals you like
You wait for the market to print sandal-money
You trade your wheat for a fixed official price in sandals
discovery.answer: You must find a cobbler who both has spare sandals and wants your wheat — a double match of wants, negotiated on the spot
discovery.hook: Barter has no price tags — one trader may give five mangoes for a kilo of rice while another demands eight. Every rate is negotiated fresh, and if nobody wants your pots, a potter cannot eat at all.

c7_eco_ch01.mission: Survive a day in a barter village — as a weaver, find who needs cloth and has what you need, then negotiate a fair swap measured in kilograms per metre.
c7_eco_ch01.finale: Money was invented because matching wants is exhausting. Barter works only when two needs collide at the same moment.

discovery.question: Riya pays a classmate 50 rupees for a handmade craft in a school corridor — no shop, no signboard, no receipt. Did a market just happen?
options: Yes — a buyer, a seller, and an exchange of value are all a market needs, whether it is a corridor, a haat, or an app
No — markets require registered shops and computers
No — 50 rupees is too small to count
Only if a teacher supervises the deal
discovery.answer: Yes — a buyer, a seller, and an exchange of value are all a market needs, whether it is a corridor, a haat, or an app
discovery.hook: A market is an arrangement, not a building. A vegetable stall and a shopping app do the same job — bringing buyer and seller together — and strictly speaking, even money is optional where value can still be exchanged.

c7_eco_ch02.mission: Audit five everyday scenes — a mandi, a phone app, a school swap day, a cobbler, a rickshaw ride — and decide which truly qualify as markets and why.
c7_eco_ch02.finale: Wherever a want meets an offer and value changes hands, a market quietly exists — no walls required.

discovery.question: A potter makes perfect pots, yet loses ten percent of every shipment because a broken dirt road rattles his trucks for six hours. Nothing is wrong with the pots — so what is actually broken?
options: The physical infrastructure — roads, power, and water systems are the skeleton under every business, and cracks in it shake the whole economy
The pots — they need better clay
The trucks — they should drive slower
Nothing — bad luck breaks pottery
discovery.answer: The physical infrastructure — roads, power, and water systems are the skeleton under every business, and cracks in it shake the whole economy
discovery.hook: Infrastructure is not a consumer good you buy at a shop — it is the shared framework that lets everything else happen. Pave the road and the same potter suddenly delivers faster, cheaper, and whole.

c7_eco_ch03.mission: Follow one glass of clean water home — count every pipe, wire, road, and pole it needed — then total what a broken road costs the potter in a single day.
c7_eco_ch03.finale: You rarely notice infrastructure until it fails. Roads and wires do not make products — they make products possible.

discovery.question: A town of 5,000 people has no bank, no payment app, no credit — savings sleep in mattresses and every deal needs a sack of cash. What invisible machinery has stopped working?
options: The financial infrastructure — without banks and payment networks, savings cannot be pooled, businesses cannot borrow, and money cannot move safely
The physical infrastructure — the roads must have vanished too
Nothing — mattresses are safer than banks anyway
The market — trade is impossible without rupees printed locally
discovery.answer: The financial infrastructure — without banks and payment networks, savings cannot be pooled, businesses cannot borrow, and money cannot move safely
discovery.hook: Banks and payment systems are the plumbing of an economy — as essential as roads are to trucks. A digital scan at a vegetable stall rides on a vast hidden network of institutions and rules, not magic.

c7_eco_ch04.mission: Design a financial rescue kit for a remote hill village — pick the three pieces of money-moving machinery it needs first and explain the job of each.
c7_eco_ch04.finale: Roads carry the goods; banks and payment networks carry the money. Break either one and trade limps to a halt.

discovery.question: In a coastal village, the high tide swallows the footpaths and the children simply wait for the water to fall. Is this setting just a pretty postcard — or something with real power over the story?
options: It is an active force — tides, floods, and isolation decide how villagers travel, work, and whether children reach a school
Just a backdrop — the same story could happen anywhere
A decoration — rivers are added to stories to sound nice
A mistake — real rivers never affect villages
discovery.answer: It is an active force — tides, floods, and isolation decide how villagers travel, work, and whether children reach a school
