discovery.hook: A setting is never window dressing. When a river floods the only path to school, geography becomes an obstacle in the plot — move the village to a dry plain and the whole struggle dissolves.

c7_engl_ch01.mission: Walk the riverbank at high tide and low tide — list what each state of the water allows or forbids — and prove the setting is steering the plot.
c7_engl_ch01.finale: Read the water and you read the village. In this story, the river does not just flow beside the characters — it pushes their lives around.

discovery.question: A respected human doctor loses every patient because his house overflows with ducks, pigs, and owls — and he chooses the animals anyway. Is he just eccentric, or is something deeper going on?
options: His radical empathy is a moral choice — he values the wellbeing of animals above wealth, reputation, and polite society
He is simply bad at business and cannot help it
He lost his medical license for incompetence
He is collecting animals to sell them later
discovery.answer: His radical empathy is a moral choice — he values the wellbeing of animals above wealth, reputation, and polite society
discovery.hook: Dr Dolittle is not merely a funny pet collector. Losing income, patients, and social standing are sacrifices — and when his parrot teaches him that animals have their own language, pets become voices worth listening to, not objects.

c7_engl_ch02.mission: Build the case for Dr Dolittle — gather three sacrifices he makes for animals and one moment an animal teaches him, then argue whether leaving human medicine was wisdom or folly.
c7_engl_ch02.finale: Real character hides in what a person gives up. Dolittle traded status for compassion — and found his true calling in the bargain.

discovery.question: A boy builds a burglar alarm that soaks his father and wakes the whole house — then starts sketching the next gadget before the floor is even dry. Is he a pest, or a budding engineer?
options: A budding inventor — relentless curiosity and resilience turn every disaster into fuel for the next experiment
A pest — anyone whose inventions fail is just careless
A dreamer — he should give up machines for something safer
A copycat — he is only repeating things he saw elsewhere
discovery.answer: A budding inventor — relentless curiosity and resilience turn every disaster into fuel for the next experiment
discovery.hook: Failure is not foolishness. A room scattered with wires and half-built gadgets mirrors a mind that prioritizes creating over tidying — and real invention has always advanced by trial and error.

c7_engl_ch03.mission: Examine the evidence — the messy workshop, the soaked father, the immediate next plan — and write a character verdict on the young inventor that weighs both the chaos and the brilliance.
c7_engl_ch03.finale: Every inventor has a trail of glorious disasters behind them. The mess is not the opposite of genius — it is the workshop of it.

discovery.question: A character steps off a sunlit railway embankment into the mouth of a brick tunnel — and in one step the birdcalls fade to hollow echoes and the heat drops away. What did the author just do to the mood?
options: Flipped it — the contrast between bright living jungle and dark silent tunnel turns open warmth into tense suspense
Nothing — a tunnel is just a shorter road
Made it cheerful — shade is always relaxing
Confused it — good authors avoid strong contrasts
discovery.answer: Flipped it — the contrast between bright living jungle and dark silent tunnel turns open warmth into tense suspense
discovery.hook: Setting is an experience built from senses, not a label on a map. Here three elements do the work — the wild jungle, the human-made railway slicing through it, and a tunnel that swallows light and sound like a quiet antagonist.

c7_engl_ch04.mission: Walk the three settings in order — jungle, railway, tunnel — and collect one sight, one sound, and one feeling from each to show how the mood darkens with every step.
c7_engl_ch04.finale: A great setting does not sit behind the story — it presses on the characters. Civilization and wilderness meet at the tunnel mouth, and the tunnel wins the mood.

discovery.question: A soldier at a far border post could send a quick digital message — but instead writes a letter beginning with three words that change everything: a greeting so warm the family reads it twice. Why does the handwritten letter matter more?
options: It carries physical intimacy — handwriting, ink, and a moment frozen in paper that digital messages cannot hold
It is faster than any phone
It costs nothing at all to send
It is required by military law
discovery.answer: It carries physical intimacy — handwriting, ink, and a moment frozen in paper that digital messages cannot hold
discovery.hook: Letter format is only the envelope — the heart of a letter is the emotion inside. An affectionate opening sets an intimate tone, and literature loves letters because they reveal inner thoughts with no narrator filtering them.

c7_engl_ch05.mission: Write the opening paragraph of a letter from a soldier to a younger sibling — balance warmth with duty — then mark the salutation, the reassurance, and the feeling hiding between the lines.
c7_engl_ch05.finale: A letter is a conversation across distance that you can hold in your hands. Long after the ink dries, the feeling stays.

discovery.question: The sun rises over Arunachal Pradesh almost two hours before it reaches Gujarat — yet both states read the exact same clock time. Where do those missing two hours hide?
options: In longitude — India spans about 30 degrees, Earth turns one degree every 4 minutes, and a single standard meridian keeps the whole country on one clock
In latitude — the east is simply closer to the sun
Nowhere — the sun rises everywhere in India at the same moment
In the mountains — the Himalayas delay the sunlight
discovery.answer: In longitude — India spans about 30 degrees, Earth turns one degree every 4 minutes, and a single standard meridian keeps the whole country on one clock
discovery.hook: Latitude and longitude do different jobs: latitude sets climate (8 to 37 degrees North gives India tropical-to-temperate zones), while longitude sets time. Mixing them up is the classic map-reading trap.

c7_geo_ch01.mission: Plot India on the degree grid — stretch from 8 N to 37 N and 68 E to 97 E — then calculate why 30 degrees of longitude costs the east two hours of morning sun.
c7_geo_ch01.finale: Every country has a grid address. Read the latitude for its seasons and the longitude for its sunrise — India runs on both at once.

discovery.question: On a clear, still winter morning a friend looks outside and announces there is no weather today. What are they completely missing?
options: Weather is always happening — temperature, wind, humidity, and pressure are all at work even when the sky is calm
Nothing — calm air really does mean no weather
They are right — weather only exists when it rains or storms
Weather only counts at night
discovery.answer: Weather is always happening — temperature, wind, humidity, and pressure are all at work even when the sky is calm
discovery.hook: Weather is not just rain-versus-shine. It is the combined state of all the elements of the atmosphere at once — which is why two neighbouring cities can have completely different weather on the very same afternoon.

c7_geo_ch02.mission: Build a school weather chart — track temperature, wind, humidity, and rainfall twice a day — and catch the atmosphere changing even on the quietest days.
c7_geo_ch02.finale: There is never no weather — only weather you have not measured yet. The sky is always up to something.

discovery.question: Rajasthan gets one unusually rainy March week, and a student declares the desert climate officially over. What is the flaw in the verdict?
options: One wet week is weather — climate is the average pattern over 30 years, so a single odd spell changes nothing
No flaw — one rainy week really can end a desert
The rain was fake — deserts cannot get rain
Climate changes every season anyway
discovery.answer: One wet week is weather — climate is the average pattern over 30 years, so a single odd spell changes nothing
discovery.hook: Weather is the outfit you wear today; climate is the whole wardrobe built over decades. A freezing January in a subtropical city does not rewrite its climate any more than one rain shower rewrites a desert.

c7_geo_ch03.mission: Sort a pile of statements — today is 34 degrees, monsoon arrives each June, a freak hailstorm hit Tuesday — into weather and climate, then defend the 30-year rule.
c7_geo_ch03.finale: Weather is the event; climate is the rule. Never let one odd afternoon overrule thirty years of evidence.

discovery.question: India has tractors, tube wells, and fertilizer factories — yet farmers still scan the June sky with worry. Why is Indian farming still called a gamble with the monsoon?
options: Most fields still depend on the timing and volume of seasonal rain — technology helps but cannot replace the water cycle
Because farmers refuse to use machines
Because monsoons are a myth invented by the news
Because tractors break down in rain
discovery.answer: Most fields still depend on the timing and volume of seasonal rain — technology helps but cannot replace the water cycle
discovery.hook: Indian farming is not one uniform system. The flat, silt-rich Northern Plains allow big irrigated fields, while the rocky Peninsular Plateau and arid Rajasthan farm under totally different rules — geography writes the farming manual.

c7_geo_ch04.mission: Compare two farms — one on the fertile Ganga plain, one on the dry plateau edge — and decide which physical gift and which human effort each one needs to succeed.
c7_geo_ch04.finale: Farming is a partnership: the land offers soil and water, the farmer offers labour and timing. The monsoon still holds the deciding vote.

discovery.question: Sri Lanka shares not a single kilometre of land border with India — the sea lies between them. So why do geographers still count it among the neighbours of India?
options: Because it sits just across the narrow Palk Strait — maritime proximity and a shared ocean zone make it a neighbour without a land border
They do not — only land borders make neighbours
Because it was once joined by a bridge, so it counts forever
Because maps are drawn too small to show the gap
discovery.answer: Because it sits just across the narrow Palk Strait — maritime proximity and a shared ocean zone make it a neighbour without a land border
discovery.hook: Borders are not random ruler lines — many follow nature itself, like the Himalayan crest separating India from China. And neighbourship does not end at the shoreline: rivers and oceans connect countries as much as they divide them.

c7_geo_ch05.mission: Sort the neighbours of India into two teams — those sharing a land border and those across the water — then trace which natural feature forms each land boundary.
c7_geo_ch05.finale: A neighbour is not just who shares your wall — it is who shares your mountains, rivers, and seas. Water separates the land but not the neighbourhood.

discovery.question: A thousand years after the Harappan cities crumbled, brand-new towns began blooming along the Ganga around 600 BCE. What single technology helped wake the cities back up?
options: Iron — axes cleared the dense forests and ploughshares turned the heavy soil, growing a food surplus that fed traders and artisans
Bronze — shinier tools attracted city builders
Fire — cooking grain invented the city
Boats — rivers alone built the towns
discovery.answer: Iron — axes cleared the dense forests and ploughshares turned the heavy soil, growing a food surplus that fed traders and artisans
discovery.hook: It is called the Second Urbanisation because the Harappan cities were the first — and they had declined over a thousand years earlier. The new towns rose in a different river valley, powered by surplus grain that freed people to become craftspersons and merchants.

c7_hist_ch01.mission: Follow an iron axe into the Gangetic forest — clear the land, grow the surplus, and trace how that surplus gathers potters, weavers, and traders into a new town.
c7_hist_ch01.finale: Cities are grown, not built. Clear the forest, fill the granary, and the marketplace assembles itself.

discovery.question: What really turns a small mahajanapada into a vast empire — one glorious battle, or something much quieter happening in the fields first?
options: Agricultural surplus paid as taxes funds a standing army and royal officials — empires are built on grain before swords
One brave king and one huge victory are all it takes
Empires appear when maps get bigger
Crowns — whoever forges the largest crown rules the most land
discovery.answer: Agricultural surplus paid as taxes funds a standing army and royal officials — empires are built on grain before swords
discovery.hook: An empire is not just a kingdom that won extra battles — it needs centralised tax collection, permanent officials, and uniform law across many regions. Magadha had the winning combination: fertile soil and iron mines beneath it.

c7_hist_ch02.mission: Audit Magadha like a royal advisor — count the iron ore, the river-fed fields, and the tax channels — and explain why this kingdom, above its rivals, was built to become an empire.
c7_hist_ch02.finale: Swords win battles; harvests win empires. The army marches on grain collected long before the war began.

discovery.question: The giant Mauryan Empire collapses into rival regional kingdoms — it sounds like a dark age, yet markets boomed, coins multiplied, and new art styles flowered. Why did breaking apart energise the subcontinent?
options: Regional rulers competed to attract merchants — patronising craft guilds, minting coins, and guarding trade routes to grow their own economies
It did not — everything fell into ruin
Foreign invaders ran every market single-handedly
The empire secretly kept ruling from hiding
discovery.answer: Regional rulers competed to attract merchants — patronising craft guilds, minting coins, and guarding trade routes to grow their own economies
discovery.hook: Political fragmentation is not the same as decline. Post-Maurya coins carried two languages and gods from different cultures on a single piece of metal — evidence of an age of reorganisation, not a dark age.

c7_hist_ch03.mission: Hold a bilingual coin from this era — decode what its two scripts and mixed deities reveal — then argue why the post-Maurya centuries deserve the name Age of Reorganisation.
c7_hist_ch03.finale: When one centre of power dissolves, many centres of creativity ignite. The map fragmented; the civilisation diversified.

discovery.question: A family of small-time local chiefs in Magadha ends up ruling an empire within a few generations — no single overnight conquest. What slow moves lifted the Guptas from Maharaja to Maharajadhiraja?
options: A fertile home base plus smart marriage alliances — the wedding of Chandragupta I to the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi raised the dynasty to imperial status
A secret treasure vault bought the throne
They conquered all of India in one campaign
A foreign emperor gifted them the crown
discovery.answer: A fertile home base plus smart marriage alliances — the wedding of Chandragupta I to the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi raised the dynasty to imperial status
discovery.hook: Empires rarely erupt overnight. Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha spent generations as local Maharajas first — and the gold coins showing the king beside queen Kumaradevi prove how precious that alliance was to their legitimacy.

c7_hist_ch04.mission: Read the evidence like a historian — early Maharaja titles, the Magadha heartland, a coin showing king and queen — and reconstruct how local chiefs became emperors.
c7_hist_ch04.finale: A title tells a story: Maharaja to Maharajadhiraja is a climb of decades, built on harvests and alliances before a single army marched.

discovery.question: Millions revere the Ganga as a living goddess, yet the village well down the lane stays just a well. How does a river — water and silt — become sacred?
options: Communities depended on it for water, fertile soil, and travel — and generations of gratitude, stories, and rituals turned that dependence into reverence
A king once declared it holy and everyone obeyed
It is the biggest river, and biggest is always sacred
Priests invented the idea for donations
discovery.answer: Communities depended on it for water, fertile soil, and travel — and generations of gratitude, stories, and rituals turned that dependence into reverence
discovery.hook: Sacredness was not decreed from above — it grew from daily survival. And shared pilgrimage routes did quiet political work: people from rival kingdoms walked to the same holy sites, stitching a divided land into one cultural fabric.

c7_hist_ch05.mission: Trace how a life-giving river becomes a goddess — list what it gives a village, then follow the pilgrims whose shared journeys wove separate kingdoms into a common sacred map.
c7_hist_ch05.finale: A river that keeps you alive is easy to love and easy to worship. Sacred geography is gratitude written onto the land.

discovery.question: When the Gupta empire weakened around the 6th century, its own governors and military chiefs — the samantas — quietly became independent kings. What made that possible?
options: Kings had begun paying officials with land grants instead of coins, so local chiefs controlled revenue and armies of their own — and stopped sending tribute
The samantas invented a new religion first
All the emperors simply forgot to collect taxes
Foreign powers appointed each samanta as king
discovery.answer: Kings had begun paying officials with land grants instead of coins, so local chiefs controlled revenue and armies of their own — and stopped sending tribute
discovery.hook: Fragmentation was not a dark age. As the centre faded, regional languages, temple styles, and local economies flourished — power scattered into many capitals, and culture scattered with it.

c7_hist_ch06.mission: Track the cracks in the clay pot — from fading coinage to land-grant payments to samantas declaring independence — then find three regional cultures that bloomed in the pieces.
c7_hist_ch06.finale: When a big pot cracks, it does not vanish — it becomes many smaller vessels. Each regional kingdom carried its own art, language, and pride.

discovery.question: Mahmud of Ghazni raided rich temple cities again and again yet never stayed to rule — while a century later Muhammad Ghuri came and founded a lasting power. What changed between the raider and the conqueror?
options: Ghazni wanted plunder; Ghuri wanted territory — and rival regional kingdoms, too divided to unite, could not stop his fast-moving cavalry
Ghazni was scared of elephants; Ghuri was not
Nothing changed — both came to conquer
Ghuri arrived with a larger navy
discovery.answer: Ghazni wanted plunder; Ghuri wanted territory — and rival regional kingdoms, too divided to unite, could not stop his fast-moving cavalry
discovery.hook: These centuries were not simply doom. While frontier cities suffered raids, interior kingdoms raised magnificent temples and thriving markets — and slow war elephants met their match in swift horse archers.

c7_hist_ch07.mission: Compare the two northwestern invaders — their goals, their tactics, their aftermath — and explain how political rivalry among regional kingdoms left the door open.
c7_hist_ch07.finale: A raider takes the treasure and leaves; a conqueror takes the throne. Divided rivals learned the difference at Tarain.

discovery.question: Centuries ago, families fleeing persecution sailed to the Malabar coast — and local rulers let them settle, trade, and worship in peace. Why would kings welcome complete strangers?
options: Welcoming migrants was smart statecraft — traders and skilled settlers enriched the economy, and a long ethos of tolerance let newcomers thrive
The rulers were tricked and could not stop them
Only because the migrants promised to give up all their customs
They were not welcomed — every arrival was an invasion
discovery.answer: Welcoming migrants was smart statecraft — traders and skilled settlers enriched the economy, and a long ethos of tolerance let newcomers thrive
discovery.hook: Not every outsider arrived with an army. Most came as traders or refugees through sea routes and mountain passes — and migration flowed both ways: newcomers adopted local language and food while adding their own crafts, faiths, and flavours to the mosaic.

c7_hist_ch08.mission: Sort the arrivals — merchant ships, refugee families, conquering armies — then show how geography, from the Khyber Pass to the monsoon sea routes, made India both reachable and welcoming.
c7_hist_ch08.finale: India was never one thread — it is a fabric woven from many arrivals. Those who came for shelter stayed to become part of the pattern.

discovery.question: A bicycle is priced 1,00,000 rupees. One friend calls it ten thousand, another calls it a crore. How does one well-placed comma settle the argument?
options: In the Indian system the comma after the lakh place shows 1,00,000 — six digits, one hundred thousand
Count the zeros — five zeros always means crore
Read it digit by digit — each 0 is worth ten
The longest number on the tag always wins
discovery.answer: In the Indian system the comma after the lakh place shows 1,00,000 — six digits, one hundred thousand
discovery.hook: Every step left on the place value chart multiplies by ten: ten ten-thousands make one lakh, and one lakh holds one hundred thousands. In the Indian system, commas come after thousands, then lakhs, then crores.

c7_math_ch01.mission: Take the number 2,35,460 and hunt down the value of the digit 2 — then prove how many thousands and how many ten-thousands hide inside one lakh.
c7_math_ch01.finale: Big numbers stop being scary when the commas do the grouping. One lakh is not a mountain — it is just ten ten-thousands standing in a row.

discovery.question: Two students count the terms in 15 + 4 x 3 - 8. One says five terms, the other says three. Who is counting right — and what trick decides it?
options: Three — multiplication glues 4 x 3 into a single term, and only plus and minus signs split terms
Five — every number separated by any symbol is its own term
Four — the minus sign does not count as a separator
One — the whole expression is always one big term
discovery.answer: Three — multiplication glues 4 x 3 into a single term, and only plus and minus signs split terms
discovery.hook: Terms are the chunks separated by + and - ; anything held together by x or division rides as one block. And watch parentheses: 40 - 5 x 6 gives 10, but (40 - 5) x 6 gives 210 — same digits, different story.

c7_math_ch02.mission: Write a shop bill as an expression — 3 notebooks at 25 each plus 2 pens at 10 each — mark its terms, then evaluate the total without mixing the order.
c7_math_ch02.finale: An expression is a sentence and terms are its words. Learn where one term ends and the next begins, and no long calculation can ambush you.

discovery.question: Your notebook edge lands somewhere between 14 cm and 15 cm — not quite either. Whole numbers just gave up. What rescues the measurement?
options: Divide one centimetre into 10 equal smaller parts — tenths fill the gap between the whole numbers
Round up to 15 and hope nobody checks
Use two rulers side by side
Declare the notebook unmeasurable
discovery.answer: Divide one centimetre into 10 equal smaller parts — tenths fill the gap between the whole numbers
discovery.hook: More divisions mean smaller units — a hundredth is tinier than a tenth, not bigger. And 4.2 rupees is 4 whole rupees plus two-tenths of one rupee — 20 paise — not six whole rupees.

c7_math_ch03.mission: Measure a pencil that lands between two marks — split the centimetre into tenths, write the length as a whole plus a fraction, and explain why whole numbers alone could not say it.
c7_math_ch03.finale: The real world lives between the whole numbers. Slice the units finer, and every in-between length finally has a name.

discovery.question: A canteen sells samosas at 15 rupees each, so the bill is 15y. Priya insists the letter y must secretly equal 5. Is she right?
options: No — y is a variable that can be 1, 2, 10, or any number of samosas; that is exactly what makes it useful
Yes — every letter hides one fixed answer
Yes — but only on days when samosas cost 15
No — y must always be zero until proven otherwise
discovery.answer: No — y is a variable that can be 1, 2, 10, or any number of samosas; that is exactly what makes it useful
discovery.hook: A letter-number is a placeholder, not a puzzle answer. That is why 4 x m = 20 is more powerful than 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 — the first describes one case, the second describes a rule that fits countless cases.

c7_math_ch04.mission: Turn three everyday situations — stamps given away, notebooks bought, kilometres travelled — into expressions with a letter for the part that can change.
c7_math_ch04.finale: Arithmetic answers one question; a variable answers all of them at once. Letters are just numbers waiting for their turn.

discovery.question: Two straight roads cross at a junction, and a friend claims that if the roads were longer they could cross a second time. Why can two straight lines never meet twice?
options: Two straight lines can share exactly one point — to cross again they would have to bend, and bending makes them no longer straight
They can — if the paper is big enough
They cross twice whenever both lines are long
Straight lines never cross at all
discovery.answer: Two straight lines can share exactly one point — to cross again they would have to bend, and bending makes them no longer straight
discovery.hook: Wherever two lines cross, they always carve out four angles around the point — even a perfect perpendicular crossing makes four right angles, not two. Three lines can share one point too, if they are concurrent.

c7_math_ch05.mission: Draw two intersecting lines, label the point of intersection, count and name all four angles — then try to make three lines share a single crossing point.
c7_math_ch05.finale: One crossing, one point, four angles. Straight lines are honest — they meet once and never double back.

discovery.question: The metro board shows arrivals at 5, 10, 15, 20 minutes. How do you already know the next train is at 25 — without waiting to see it?
options: The sequence follows a rule — +5 each time — so the rule predicts every future term without listing them
It is luck — the pattern could break any second
The board is programmed to fool passengers
You add all the numbers shown to get the next
discovery.answer: The sequence follows a rule — +5 each time — so the rule predicts every future term without listing them
discovery.hook: Not every sequence adds the same step. Check the gaps: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26 grows by +3, +5, +7, +9 — the differences themselves are growing, so guessing add-3 forever fails.

c7_math_ch06.mission: Crack three sequences — one adding a constant, one doubling, one with growing gaps — write the rule of each, then jump straight to the tenth term of the first.
c7_math_ch06.finale: A sequence is a rule wearing a number costume. Find the rule once, and every future term is already yours.

discovery.question: You have two straight sticks and try to fence off a flat region on your desk. No matter how you place them, space stays open. Why does closing a shape demand at least three sticks?
options: Two segments can only make an angle or an open path — three is the minimum needed to close a boundary, and that shape is a triangle
Two sticks can close a shape if they are long enough
One stick can close a shape if it bends
You need four — three is too few
discovery.answer: Two segments can only make an angle or an open path — three is the minimum needed to close a boundary, and that shape is a triangle
discovery.hook: The triangle is the simplest closed polygon: exactly 3 vertices, 3 straight sides, 3 interior angles. Curve one side and it stops being a triangle — and side AB is the same segment as BA, just named from the other end.

c7_math_ch07.mission: Name a triangle PQR completely — list its three vertices, three sides, and three angles — then explain why a shape with one curved side fails the test.
c7_math_ch07.finale: Three sticks, three corners, one closed region — the triangle is where all of geometry begins.

discovery.question: After the farewell party three-fourths of the cake remains, and you are offered half of the leftover. Do you end up with more or less than 3/4 — and why does multiplying fractions shrink the prize?
options: Less — half of 3/4 is 3/8, because multiplying means taking a portion of a portion
More — multiplication always makes things bigger
Exactly 3/4 — halves cancel out
The same as half a cake — leftovers do not count
discovery.answer: Less — half of 3/4 is 3/8, because multiplying means taking a portion of a portion
discovery.hook: Fraction multiplication ignores common denominators — multiply straight across, top with top and bottom with bottom. And a whole number joins in as itself over 1: 2/3 x 4 is 8/3, not 8/12.

c7_math_ch08.mission: Solve a tailor problem — find 2/3 of a 3/4 metre cloth strip — then discover what happens every time a fraction meets its own flipped reciprocal.
c7_math_ch08.finale: Multiplying fractions is sharing a share. The product of two proper fractions is always smaller than either — because a piece of a piece is a smaller piece.

discovery.question: Two equilateral triangles both have perfect 60-degree angles — but one has 4 cm sides and the other 8 cm. Geometric twins, or just lookalikes?
options: Lookalikes — congruence demands the same shape AND the same size, and 4 cm does not equal 8 cm
Twins — matching angles is all congruence needs
Twins — any two equilateral triangles are congruent
Neither is a real triangle
discovery.answer: Lookalikes — congruence demands the same shape AND the same size, and 4 cm does not equal 8 cm
discovery.hook: Congruent means one figure can be laid exactly over the other — every side and angle matching. Beware the reverse trap too: two shapes can share the same perimeter or area and still not be congruent.

c7_math_ch09.mission: Play congruence detective — test two line segments, two angles, and two cut pieces of a 24 square-centimetre rectangle — and declare which pairs truly match edge to edge.
c7_math_ch09.finale: Same shape is only half the test — same size seals it. Congruent figures are geometric identical twins.

discovery.question: A weather app shows Shimla at -4 degrees and Srinagar at -7 degrees. A friend says Shimla is colder because 4 is less than 7. Settle the argument with the number line.
options: Srinagar is colder — -7 sits further left of zero than -4, and leftward always means smaller
Shimla is colder — 4 is the smaller digit
Both are equally cold — negatives are all the same
Shimla is colder — smaller numbers are always colder
discovery.answer: Srinagar is colder — -7 sits further left of zero than -4, and leftward always means smaller
discovery.hook: Zero is the neutral border, neither positive nor negative. An elevator proves the logic: up 5, down 8, up 3 lands you right back at 0 — every step is just a signed number doing its job.

c7_math_ch10.mission: Ride the floors — start at ground 0, go up 5, down 8, up 3 — then rank three negative temperatures from warmest to coldest on the number line.
c7_math_ch10.finale: On the left of zero, bigger digits mean smaller values. The minus sign reverses everything — that is its whole job.

discovery.question: You have 12 red flags and 18 blue flags and must arrange both colours into identical equal rows with none left over. Which row sizes actually work?
options: 1, 2, 3, or 6 flags per row — the common factors that divide both 12 and 18 exactly
Any size — just make the rows roughly even
Only 12 — the bigger number decides
4 or 9 — they feel like nice divisors
discovery.answer: 1, 2, 3, or 6 flags per row — the common factors that divide both 12 and 18 exactly
discovery.hook: Common factors live where two factor lists overlap — and a factor can never exceed the number it divides. And 1 always makes the list, since it divides every whole number.

c7_math_ch11.mission: List every factor of 24 and every factor of 36, circle where the lists overlap, and then check whether 3 really deserves a place among the common factors of 15 and 25.
c7_math_ch11.finale: Finding common factors is a matching game — list both sides, keep the overlap, and never let a number divide what it cannot.

discovery.question: A student sorts 0.5, 0.45, and 0.512 by peeking at the last digit of each and gets the order wrong. What one move makes decimal sorting foolproof?
options: Pad every decimal to the same number of places — 0.500, 0.450, 0.512 — then compare like whole numbers
Always trust the longest decimal to be biggest
Compare only the first digit after the point
Sort by the number of digits — fewer means smaller
discovery.answer: Pad every decimal to the same number of places — 0.500, 0.450, 0.512 — then compare like whole numbers
discovery.hook: Each step right of the decimal point divides by ten — tenths, hundredths, thousandths. In 8.452, the digit 4 is worth 200 times the digit 2. Face value means nothing; place value is everything.

c7_math_ch12.mission: Turn 5 and 3/8 into a decimal by aiming for a denominator of 1000, then rank three tricky decimals by equalising their decimal places first.
c7_math_ch12.finale: The decimal point is an anchor — wholes on the left, shrinking pieces on the right. Equalise the places and every comparison turns honest.

discovery.question: Two questions: How many pens does Priya have in her pencil box? and How many pens do Class 7 students carry? One is a statistics question, the other is not. Which is which — and what decides?
options: The Class 7 question is statistical — it expects a variety of answers across a group, while Priya alone has one fixed answer
The Priya question is statistical — bags and boxes always vary
Both are statistical — any question with a number counts
Neither — statistics only happens in labs
discovery.answer: The Class 7 question is statistical — it expects a variety of answers across a group, while Priya alone has one fixed answer
discovery.hook: A statistical question must anticipate variability — different answers from different people. Even a changing topic fails the test if the question asks for just one value, like the single hottest temperature in May.

c7_math_ch13.mission: Sort six questions into statistical and not — from the capital of India to weekly TV hours of Grade 7 — then rewrite one boring question to make it statistical.
c7_math_ch13.finale: Statistics begins with a question that can disagree with itself. Ask a group, expect variety — ask one person, expect a number.

discovery.question: You must copy a 6.2 cm line segment exactly — but this time no reading numbers off a ruler scale. How did ancient builders pull off perfect copies anyway?
options: Set the compass span on the original segment, lift it, and swing — the fixed compass width transfers the length with no numbers needed
Fold the paper until the ends touch
Estimate by eye and hope for close
Trace it with string and guess the knots
discovery.answer: Set the compass span on the original segment, lift it, and swing — the fixed compass width transfers the length with no numbers needed
discovery.hook: Classical construction allows only two tools — a straightedge for lines and a compass for distance. Never widen or narrow the compass mid-task: its locked span is the guarantee that every arc point sits the same distance from the centre.

c7_math_ch14.mission: Using only compass and straightedge, verify whether two segments on your page are truly equal — then explain why a marked ruler would have spoiled the purity of the test.
c7_math_ch14.finale: Measurement counts; construction proves. A locked compass and a straight edge build exactness from pure geometry.

discovery.question: A market beam balance sits level: potatoes on one pan, iron weights on the other. Two statements — 4x + 7 and 4x + 7 = 23 — look alike, but only one can be solved for x. Which one, and why?
options: 4x + 7 = 23 — the equals sign locks a balance that forces x to one exact value, while the bare expression changes with every x you try
4x + 7 — shorter things are easier to solve
Both — any letters and numbers can be solved
Neither — equations need two variables
discovery.answer: 4x + 7 = 23 — the equals sign locks a balance that forces x to one exact value, while the bare expression changes with every x you try
discovery.hook: The equals sign does not mean write the answer here — it means the two sides weigh the same. Test any candidate by substitution: try x = 4 in 3x - 5 = 2x + 1 and the pans read 7 against 9 — not balanced, not the solution.

c7_math_ch15.mission: Hunt for the true solution — substitute candidate values into both sides of an equation, weigh LHS against RHS, and crown the x that keeps the beam level.
c7_math_ch15.finale: An expression is a price tag; an equation is a balance. Find the value that levels the pans and you have found the unknown.

discovery.question: A student predicts a toy car will roll faster on carpet than on marble — then the test proves her wrong. She calls the experiment a total failure. Is she right?
options: No — a test that disproves a guess is still a success, because it rules out a wrong idea and points to a better question
Yes — science only counts when your guess wins
Yes — she should have guessed marble first
No — but only because the car was faulty
discovery.answer: No — a test that disproves a guess is still a success, because it rules out a wrong idea and points to a better question
discovery.hook: Science begins with a curious question, not a textbook answer — then a guess, then a fair test with controlled variables, then honest records. Data, not neat notebooks, is the evidence that decides.

c7_physics_ch01.mission: Design a fair test for a bubbling kitchen question — does sunlight make water evaporate faster — controlling every variable except the one you are testing.
c7_physics_ch01.finale: In science there are no failed experiments — only answers you did not expect. Every wrong guess eliminated is progress.

discovery.question: A family plugs a room heater and a water geyser into the same socket board at once — and the wiring starts to overheat. What went wrong with such ordinary appliances?
options: Two high-power devices drew a heavy combined current that overheated the wires — a fire risk
Nothing — the switch was on, so it was safe
Geysers and heaters cancel each other out
The appliances were artificial, not natural
discovery.answer: Two high-power devices drew a heavy combined current that overheated the wires — a fire risk
discovery.hook: Electricity earns its keep by transforming — into heat in an iron, motion in a fan, light in a bulb. Copper wires carry it easily while plastic blocks it, and every socket has a safe load limit.

c7_physics_ch02.mission: Tour a household as an energy detective — match the iron, fan, bulb, and buzzer to the energy each converts electricity into, then flag the overloaded socket.
c7_physics_ch02.finale: Electricity is a shapeshifter — it arrives as current and leaves as light, heat, sound, or spin. Respect the load, or the wires pay the price.

discovery.question: Which holds more heat — a tiny cup of boiling tea or a whole swimming pool of lukewarm water? Most people pick the cup and get it wrong.
options: The pool — it holds far more water, so its total heat energy dwarfs the cup despite the lower temperature
The cup — higher temperature always means more heat
Neither — heat and temperature are the same thing
They are equal — water is water
discovery.answer: The pool — it holds far more water, so its total heat energy dwarfs the cup despite the lower temperature
discovery.hook: Temperature measures how fast particles move — the degree of hotness — while heat is the total energy on the move. Heat always flows from higher temperature to lower until both sides balance.

c7_physics_ch03.mission: Mix one litre of boiling water with one litre of cool tap water, then imagine five litres boiling instead — predict which mix ends hotter and defend it using total heat, not just temperature.
c7_physics_ch03.finale: A spark can be hotter than a bonfire and still hold less heat. Temperature is the intensity; heat is the crowd.

discovery.question: A sundial tells perfect time through a sunny afternoon — but a monsoon sky or midnight renders it blind. How did people measure the hours when the shadow disappeared?
options: With water clocks — a steady drip from a vessel marks equal time intervals no matter the weather
By guessing based on hunger
By counting heartbeats out loud
They simply waited for the sun to return
discovery.answer: With water clocks — a steady drip from a vessel marks equal time intervals no matter the weather
discovery.hook: Every early clock ran on something that changes predictably — a shadow sliding round a gnomon, or water flowing at a steady rate. And watch the shadow shrink toward noon: it is shortest when the sun stands highest.

c7_physics_ch04.mission: Build a water clock — pierce a vessel, measure how 300 mL drains in 15 minutes, then predict the drip time for 100 mL and verify the rate holds steady.
c7_physics_ch04.finale: Before gears and batteries, time was measured by whatever moved steadily — a travelling shadow or a patient drip.

discovery.question: A garden lamp soaks up sunshine all day and glows through the night on stored power. Natural light source or artificial — which team does it belong to?
options: A hybrid — the energy comes naturally from the Sun, but the LED that actually emits the light is human-made
Purely natural — sunlight powers it end to end
Purely artificial — it glows at night like a torch
Neither — stored light belongs to no category
discovery.answer: A hybrid — the energy comes naturally from the Sun, but the LED that actually emits the light is human-made
discovery.hook: The real test of a light source is emission, not glow. The Moon shines by borrowing sunlight — it reflects, never produces. A firefly, glowing by its own chemistry, is a truer source than the whole Moon.

c7_physics_ch05.mission: Sort the night sky and your house — Sun, Moon, stars, firefly, candle, LED, neon sign — into emitters and borrowers, natural and artificial, and defend each call.
c7_physics_ch05.finale: Ask any glowing thing one question: did you make this light or borrow it? Emitters pass; reflectors get caught.

discovery.question: It is noon in India — bright sun overhead — while on the far side of the planet it is midnight. Why can the whole Earth never share daytime at once?
options: Earth is an opaque spinning sphere — sunlight lights only the half facing it, and rotation carries each side through light and dark in 24 hours
Because the Sun is too small to light the whole planet
Because clouds cover half the Earth always
Because night is a shadow cast by the Moon
discovery.answer: Earth is an opaque spinning sphere — sunlight lights only the half facing it, and rotation carries each side through light and dark in 24 hours
discovery.hook: The Sun does not travel under the Earth at night — we spin. Earth rotates west to east, turning 360 degrees in 24 hours — a steady 15 degrees every hour. Stop the spin and one hemisphere would burn in endless day while the other froze in endless night.

c7_physics_ch06.mission: Take a ball and a torch in a dark room — spin the ball slowly, watch day chase night around it — then compute how many degrees your spot on Earth turns each hour.
c7_physics_ch06.finale: Day and night are not the Sun coming and going — they are you, riding a spinning planet through a beam of light.

discovery.question: Lemons and curd are acids you safely eat every day — so a student figures lab acids must be safe to taste too. What is dangerously wrong with that logic?
options: Weak organic acids in food are nothing like strong corrosive lab acids — never taste a laboratory chemical
Nothing — sour is sour, all acids are alike
Lab acids are safe if you sip slowly
Only bases are dangerous, acids are fine
discovery.answer: Weak organic acids in food are nothing like strong corrosive lab acids — never taste a laboratory chemical
discovery.hook: Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red; bases taste bitter, feel soapy, and turn red litmus blue. But senses are for kitchen clues — in the lab, indicators do the tasting for you. And distilled water? Perfectly neutral, no matter where it is stored.

c7_physics_ch07.mission: Sort a shelf of everyday liquids — lemon juice, soap solution, vinegar, distilled water — into acid, base, and neutral using only indicator clues, no tasting allowed.
c7_physics_ch07.finale: Sour suggests acid, soapy suggests base — but let litmus paper take the risk. In chemistry, curiosity should never touch the tongue.
